EncFormer: Secure and Efficient Transformer Inference over Encrypted Data

Yufan Zhu*    Chao Jin†    Khin Mi Mi Aung†    Xiaokui Xiao* ††thanks: *National University of Singapore, Singapore.††thanks: †Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), Singapore.
Abstract

Transformer inference in machine-learning-as-a-service (MLaaS) raises privacy concerns for sensitive user inputs. Prior secure solutions that combine fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) and secure multiparty computation (MPC) are bottlenecked by inefficient FHE kernels, communication-heavy MPC protocols, and expensive FHE–MPC conversions. We present EncFormer, a two-party private Transformer inference framework that introduces Stage Compatible Patterns so that FHE kernels compose efficiently, reducing repacking and conversions. EncFormer also provides a cost analysis model built around a minimal-conversion baseline, enabling principled selection of FHE–MPC boundaries. To further reduce communication, EncFormer proposes a secure complex CKKS–MPC conversion protocol and designs communication-efficient MPC protocols for nonlinearities. With GPU optimizations, evaluations on GPT- and BERT-style models show that EncFormer achieves 1.4×\times–30.4×\times lower online MPC communication and 1.3×\times–9.8×\times lower end-to-end latency against prior hybrid FHE–MPC systems, and 1.9×\times–3.5×\times lower end-to-end latency on BERT-base than FHE-only pipelines under a matched backend, while maintaining near-plaintext accuracy on selected GLUE tasks.

Index Terms: 
private inference, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, transformer inference

I Introduction

Transformer models such as BERT [1] and GPT [2] are increasingly deployed through machine-learning-as-a-service platforms, where user inputs are processed by an untrusted model provider. Sensitive domains such as clinical NLP [3], legal text [4], biomedical mining [5], and financial compliance [6] amplify the risk, as both inputs and predictions may be confidential, and attacks such as membership inference [7] can extract private information from model access alone. Private inference based on fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) and secure multiparty computation (MPC) is a natural fit, but current Transformer pipelines remain expensive because their performance depends not only on the cryptographic primitive but also on how ciphertext layouts, conversion boundaries, and nonlinear protocols interact across the pipeline [8, 9, 10, 11, 12].

Prior work on private Transformer inference follows three broad directions. FHE-only systems eliminate online interaction but pay heavily for deep ciphertext computation and, in many cases, bootstrapping [13, 11, 12]. MPC-only systems preserve accurate nonlinear computation but are dominated by repeated interaction on wide activations [14, 9]. Hybrid FHE–MPC systems balance these trade-offs by evaluating wide linear algebra under FHE and delegating nonlinear blocks to MPC, but they inherit a second design problem: every benefit from moving work across the boundary depends on whether the resulting packing can be consumed by the next stage and whether the added conversion cost is justified [15, 8, 16, 10].

I-A Challenges in Hybrid Private Transformer Inference

For hybrid pipelines, the main bottlenecks are no longer isolated to a single primitive. First, FHE kernel efficiency depends on packing compatibility across adjacent stages, because a locally efficient kernel can still lose its gain if its output must be repacked before the next FHE operation. Second, FHE–MPC conversion is expensive enough that boundary placement cannot be chosen by intuition alone: using a richer boundary representation may reduce MPC rounds, but only if the extra ciphertext payload and CKKS work are repaid by downstream savings. Third, secure conversion protocols in prior hybrid systems under-utilize CKKS complex slots by exporting only the real part, which increases boundary traffic even when the surrounding pipeline already uses complex packing.

These observations suggest that private Transformer inference should be framed as a secure systems co-design problem rather than as a collection of independent optimizations. The system must expose a consistent cross-stage packing discipline, a secure and communication-efficient conversion protocol, and a boundary decision rule that explains when a non-minimal conversion layout is worthwhile.

I-B Our Contribution

We present EncFormer, a two-party hybrid FHE–MPC framework for private Transformer inference in the semi-honest model. The client holds the private input and CKKS secret key, the server holds the model, and the full protocol composes FHE kernels, secure conversion boundaries, and MPC nonlinear blocks. Our main thesis is that hybrid inference becomes more predictable when these components are co-designed around stage compatibility and boundary cost.

We make three integrated contributions.

  • •

    Packing-co-designed FHE kernels. We introduce Stage Compatible Patterns (SCP), which restrict the pipeline to three canonical packing formats and treat packing as a cross-stage contract. Guided by SCP, EncFormer designs a shared plaintext–ciphertext projection kernel and folded-diagonal ciphertext–ciphertext attention kernels whose outputs are directly consumable by downstream stages, avoiding ciphertext remaps between adjacent FHE kernels.

  • •

    Boundary co-design and secure conversion. We introduce a secure complex CKKS–MPC conversion protocol that uses both the real and imaginary channels to carry two real vectors per ciphertext. While Powerformer uses complex numbers to fuse generic blockwise matrix permutations in its attention kernels, EncFormer instead exploits the diagonal and token-shift structure of attention to produce specialized packed layouts (folded-diagonal, head-major) that chain across stages via SCP. EncFormer also uses complex conversion at FHE–MPC boundaries to halve the conversion payload. We pair this with a calibrated decision rule for boundary placement under the validated PhantomFHE setting.

  • •

    End-to-end secure inference pipeline. We implement EncFormer on GPUs for GPT2-base, BERT-base, and BERT-large, combining FHE linear kernels with communication-efficient MPC protocols for softmax, layer normalization, and GELU. Evaluations show that EncFormer reduces online communication by 30.4×\times vs. BOLT, 2.6×\times vs. BumbleBee, and 1.4×\times vs. BLB, while improving end-to-end latency by 9.8×\times, 2.1×\times, and 1.3×\times on average, respectively. EncFormer also outperforms FHE-only pipelines on BERT-base by 3.5×\times over THOR and 1.9×\times over Powerformer under a matched backend. On BERT-base, encrypted inference maintains near-plaintext accuracy on selected GLUE tasks (SST-2, MRPC, RTE). Section II-C gives the pipeline security proof; kernel derivations, backend-specific comparisons, and supporting analytical details appear in the appendix at the end of this paper.

I-C System Overview

Figure 1 summarizes one EncFormer encoder block. The server first applies a shared plaintext–ciphertext projection kernel to produce QQ, KK, and VV in layouts chosen for their immediate consumers: QQ and KK are emitted in the score-friendly segment order, while VV is emitted in head-major order. The score kernel exports minimal folded-diagonal ciphertexts across the CKKS–MPC boundary, where the MPC softmax block operates on secret shares and returns weights in the same boundary format. The value kernel consumes these weights directly, and the output projection absorbs the remaining layout adaptation through plaintext weight pre-permutation rather than ciphertext repacking. The feed-forward projections follow the same principle, while MPC is reserved for layer normalization and GELU. This organization is the structural basis for SCP, complex conversion, and the boundary cost analysis developed in the following sections.

II Background and Threat Model

II-A Cryptographic Preliminaries

Fully Homomorphic Encryption. A public-key FHE scheme provides algorithms 𝖪𝖾𝗒𝖦𝖾𝗇→(𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄,𝖾𝗏𝗄)\mathsf{KeyGen}\!\to\!(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk},\mathsf{evk}), 𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗉𝗄​(⋅)\mathsf{Enc}_{\mathsf{pk}}(\cdot), 𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗌𝗄​(⋅)\mathsf{Dec}_{\mathsf{sk}}(\cdot), and 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅𝖾𝗏𝗄​(f,⋅)\mathsf{Eval}_{\mathsf{evk}}(f,\cdot) such that, for an arithmetic circuit ff,

𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗌𝗄​(𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅𝖾𝗏𝗄​(f,𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗉𝗄​(x)))={f⁡(x)modt,f⁡(x)+ε.\mathsf{Dec}_{\mathsf{sk}}\!\bigl(\mathsf{Eval}_{\mathsf{evk}}(f,\mathsf{Enc}_{\mathsf{pk}}(x))\bigr)=\begin{cases}f(x)\bmod t,\\ f(x)+\varepsilon.\end{cases}

The first line corresponds to exact schemes such as BFV and BGV. The second corresponds to approximate schemes such as CKKS, where ε\varepsilon captures approximation from encoding, decoding, and noise growth [17, 18, 19]. We use a leveled CKKS instantiation without bootstrapping, implemented on the GPU-accelerated libraries PhantomFHE [20] and Liberate.FHE [21]. We refer to [22, 23] for broader FHE background. The algorithm 𝖪𝖾𝗒𝖦𝖾𝗇\mathsf{KeyGen} samples a public key for encryption, a secret key for decryption, and evaluation keys derived from the secret key. In RLWE-based FHE, 𝖾𝗏𝗄\mathsf{evk} typically includes relinearization keys to manage ciphertext growth after multiplication and Galois keys that enable SIMD slot permutations such as rotations and conjugation. The algorithm 𝖤𝗇𝖼𝗉𝗄\mathsf{Enc}_{\mathsf{pk}} encodes and encrypts a plaintext into a ciphertext, 𝖤𝗏𝖺𝗅𝖾𝗏𝗄\mathsf{Eval}_{\mathsf{evk}} applies additions, multiplications, and slot permutations directly on ciphertexts using only public evaluation material, and 𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗌𝗄\mathsf{Dec}_{\mathsf{sk}} recovers the plaintext result [24, 18, 25].

Secure Multiparty Computation. Secure multiparty computation allows parties to jointly evaluate a function over private inputs while revealing only the prescribed outputs. We use two-party arithmetic secret sharing over ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}} and represent real values in fixed point with scale s=2Fs=2^{F}, where FF is the fractional bit-width and ℓ\ell is the ring bit-width. Linear maps are computed locally on shares. To multiply shared values, we use Beaver triples (a,b,c)(a,b,c) with c=a​bc=ab [26]. Given shared xx and shared yy, the parties open α=x−a\alpha=x-a and β=y−b\beta=y-b, then obtain a sharing of the product by setting z=x​yz=xy and computing

zsh=csh+α​bsh+β​ash+α​β,z^{\mathrm{sh}}=c^{\mathrm{sh}}+\alpha\,b^{\mathrm{sh}}+\beta\,a^{\mathrm{sh}}+\alpha\beta,

where the public term α​β\alpha\beta is incorporated into one party’s share. For fixed-point arithmetic, multiplying two ss-scaled values produces a value at scale s2s^{2}, so we apply an interactive secure truncation protocol that right shifts by FF bits to return to scale ss. This yields an online phase with one interaction round per multiplication depth and communication proportional to circuit size, as in SPDZ-style protocols [27]. In the semi-honest model, security is captured by the real/ideal paradigm [28, 29].

In EncFormer, we use a hybrid FHE–MPC setting. CKKS provides SIMD-style approximate arithmetic on vectors packed into ciphertext slots, supporting ciphertext addition, ciphertext/plaintext multiplication, ciphertext/ciphertext multiplication, rotations, and conjugation [19]. We adopt CKKS because Transformer inference is dominated by real-valued linear algebra and already operates in finite precision, so it tolerates small approximation error. This choice is consistent with prior hybrid FHE–MPC Transformer systems [15, 8, 10, 30]. CKKS’s scale-and-rescale workflow matches the way Transformer layers accumulate depth through chained linear maps, and its SIMD packing over complex slots enables batching and reduces ciphertext count for matrix workloads. We exploit complex packing inside our FHE kernels with SCP and at FHE–MPC conversion boundaries. For nonlinear layers, we use the MPC building blocks above. The resulting latency is sensitive to the number of rounds and the amount of data crossing each MPC boundary, which is why boundary design matters as much as primitive selection in a hybrid pipeline.

II-B CKKS Parameters

We instantiate FHE with the RNS–CKKS scheme of Cheon et al. [19], which supports approximate arithmetic on vectors packed into ciphertext slots. CKKS operates over the cyclotomic ring RQ=ℤQ​[X]/(XN+1)R_{Q}=\mathbb{Z}_{Q}[X]/(X^{N}+1) for power-of-two NN, and packs n=N/2n=N/2 complex slots via an approximate encoding map. Figure 2 illustrates the residue number system (RNS) representation and how computation proceeds across the modulus chain. In its RNS form, the ciphertext modulus is represented as a product of machine-word primes Q=∏i=0LqiQ=\prod_{i=0}^{L}q_{i}, and polynomial coefficients are stored and processed as residues modulo each qiq_{i}, enabling efficient NTT-based arithmetic and scale management across the chain.

Practical deployments fix a modulus chain Q=∏i=0LqiQ=\prod_{i=0}^{L}q_{i} and a target scale Δ\Delta sized for multiplicative depth D≤LD\leq L. Let Qi=∏j=0iqjQ_{i}=\prod_{j=0}^{i}q_{j} denote the remaining ciphertext modulus at level ii. A ciphertext–ciphertext multiplication inflates the scale by roughly a factor of Δ\Delta and is followed by 𝗋𝖾𝗌𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖾\mathsf{rescale}, which maps the ciphertext modulus from QiQ_{i} to Qi−1Q_{i-1} by dividing by qiq_{i} and restores the scale to approximately Δ\Delta. After uu multiplication–rescale steps, the remaining modulus is QL−uQ_{L-u}. Ciphertext size and remaining multiplicative depth both depend on the active level of this chain, so boundary-conversion cost depends not only on tensor shape but also on the CKKS parameters at the conversion point. Our cost model therefore treats ciphertext size as a function of the ring degree and the remaining RNS limbs.

II-C Threat Model

We consider the standard two-party private inference setting with a client P0P_{0} and a server P1P_{1}. The client provides the private input and learns the inference output; the server provides the model. We assume semi-honest adversaries: both parties follow the protocol but may try to infer additional information from the transcript. As in prior hybrid systems, the model architecture is known to both parties [31, 32, 16, 8, 10].

Key Distribution. Following prior hybrid systems [32, 8, 10, 16], the client generates the CKKS key material (𝗉𝗄,𝗌𝗄,𝖾𝗏𝗄)(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{sk},\mathsf{evk}) and sends (𝗉𝗄,𝖾𝗏𝗄)(\mathsf{pk},\mathsf{evk}) to the server, while retaining the secret key locally. This is the standard key-distribution pattern in two-party hybrid inference [32, 8, 10]: the client holds the secret key so that decryption occurs only on the client side, and the server never observes plaintext activations. During CKKS-to-MPC conversion, the client decrypts only one-time-padded ciphertexts, so the plaintext observed by either party is statistically or computationally protected by the underlying conversion protocol.

The inference protocol is organized as a sequence of components Π𝖨𝗇𝖿𝖾𝗋=Π1∘⋯∘ΠK\Pi_{\mathsf{Infer}}=\Pi_{1}\circ\cdots\circ\Pi_{K}, where each Πj\Pi_{j} is a CKKS evaluation block, an MPC block over ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}}, or an FHE–MPC conversion boundary. Every intermediate value is represented either as a CKKS ciphertext under the secret key or as additive secret shares held by the two parties.

Theorem 1 (Pipeline Security).

If CKKS is semantically secure and the MPC protocols and complex conversion protocols are secure in the semi-honest threat model, then Π𝖨𝗇𝖿𝖾𝗋\Pi_{\mathsf{Infer}} securely realizes the ideal inference functionality in the semi-honest model.

Proof.

Fix a party PbP_{b} for b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}. Let 𝗏𝗂𝖾𝗐b\mathsf{view}_{b} denote its real-execution view and 𝗈𝗎𝗍\mathsf{out} the prescribed client output. We construct a simulator 𝒮b\mathcal{S}_{b} such that {𝒮b(𝗂𝗇b,𝗈𝗎𝗍),𝗈𝗎𝗍}≡c{𝗏𝗂𝖾𝗐b,𝗈𝗎𝗍}\bigl\{\mathcal{S}_{b}(\mathsf{in}_{b},\mathsf{out}),\mathsf{out}\bigr\}\equiv_{c}\bigl\{\mathsf{view}_{b},\mathsf{out}\bigr\}. Each component Πj\Pi_{j} is secure by assumption, so it admits a simulator 𝒮b(j)\mathcal{S}^{(j)}_{b} producing a transcript indistinguishable from the real one: for CKKS blocks this follows from semantic security, for MPC blocks from semi-honest MPC security, and for conversion boundaries from Section V. The global simulator 𝒮b\mathcal{S}_{b} composes these component simulators in order. A standard hybrid argument over 𝖧0,…,𝖧K\mathsf{H}_{0},\ldots,\mathsf{H}_{K} (where 𝖧j\mathsf{H}_{j} replaces the first jj transcripts with simulated ones) yields 𝖧0≡c𝖧K\mathsf{H}_{0}\equiv_{c}\mathsf{H}_{K}, showing that the composed protocol leaks nothing beyond the prescribed output. ∎

II-D Transformer Model

The Transformer is a sequence model built around self-attention, replacing recurrence and convolution with token–token interactions that can be computed in parallel [33]. For a sequence of length mm with hidden size dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}} and activations A∈ℝm×dmodelA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}, the attention sublayer forms Q=A​WQQ=AW_{Q}, K=A​WKK=AW_{K}, and V=A​WVV=AW_{V} with WQ,WK,WV∈ℝdmodel×dmodelW_{Q},W_{K},W_{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. With HH heads of width dh=dmodel/Hd_{h}=d_{\mathrm{model}}/H, write Q(h),K(h),V(h)∈ℝm×dhQ^{(h)},K^{(h)},V^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{h}} for the hhth head slices. A compact head computation is

Att(h)=softmax⁡(Q(h)​(K(h))⊤dh)​V(h).\mathrm{Att}^{(h)}\;=\;\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q^{(h)}(K^{(h)})^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\right)V^{(h)}.

The multi-head output concatenates all heads and applies an output projection WO∈ℝdmodel×dmodelW_{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_{\mathrm{model}}},

MHA⁡(A)=Concat⁡(Att(0),…,Att(H−1))​WO.\mathrm{MHA}(A)\;=\;\mathrm{Concat}\!\bigl(\mathrm{Att}^{(0)},\dots,\mathrm{Att}^{(H-1)}\bigr)W_{O}.

This is followed by a position-wise feed-forward sublayer FFN⁡(x)=ϕ⁡(x​W1+b1)​W2+b2\mathrm{FFN}(x)=\phi(xW_{1}+b_{1})W_{2}+b_{2} using ϕ=GELU\phi=\mathrm{GELU}, with residual connections and layer normalization throughout [33]. Figure 3 shows the reference architecture used in this work.

BERT is an encoder-only Transformer that stacks NLN_{L} identical layers to build bidirectional context [1]. We evaluate BERT-base with NL=12N_{L}=12, dmodel=768d_{\mathrm{model}}=768, intermediate size 30723072, and H=12H=12, and BERT-large with NL=24N_{L}=24, dmodel=1024d_{\mathrm{model}}=1024, intermediate size 40964096, and H=16H=16, where both have dh=64d_{h}=64. We also evaluate GPT2-base, a decoder-only Transformer with causal self-attention [2], which matches BERT-base in NLN_{L}, dmodeld_{\mathrm{model}}, HH, and intermediate size. These dimensions determine the packing sizes, boundary tensor shapes, and kernel schedules used in the later sections.

III Packing-Co-Designed FHE Kernels

This section presents the FHE side of EncFormer. We first define the packing notation and CKKS primitives used by the kernels, then introduce Stage Compatible Patterns (SCP) as the cross-stage layout discipline, and finally describe the shared projection kernel and the ciphertext–ciphertext attention kernels.

A key computational characteristic of the Transformer architecture is the attention block in Section II-D, whose runtime is dominated by large linear projections and matrix multiplications. Following prior hybrid Transformer systems [15, 8, 30, 16, 10], EncFormer evaluates these linear components under FHE.

III-A Packing Model and Stage Compatibility

Let nn denote the number of slots in one CKKS ciphertext. We partition the nn slots into Nseg=n/mN_{\mathrm{seg}}=n/m contiguous segments, each containing mm slots, so that m​Nseg=nmN_{\mathrm{seg}}=n. We write bold lowercase letters for slot vectors in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. For a vector 𝐯∈ℂn\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}, we denote its CKKS encryption by ⟨𝐯⟩\langle\mathbf{v}\rangle. For 𝐯,𝐰∈ℂn\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}, we use 𝐯+𝐰\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w} and 𝐯⊙𝐰\mathbf{v}\odot\mathbf{w} for elementwise addition and multiplication, and 𝐯¯\overline{\mathbf{v}} for complex conjugation. Let ρ⁡(𝐯,r)\rho(\mathbf{v};r) denote the cyclic left shift of 𝐯\mathbf{v} by rr positions, where r∈ℤr\in\mathbb{Z} and indices are taken modulo nn.

ρ⁡(𝐯,r)=(vr,vr+1,…,vn−1,v0,…,vr−1).\rho(\mathbf{v};r)\;=\;(v_{r},v_{r+1},\dots,v_{n-1},v_{0},\dots,v_{r-1}).

To express segment structure, let 𝐱∈ℂn\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{n} be a slot vector and index slots by a within-segment coordinate r∈{0,…,m−1}r\in\{0,\dots,m-1\} and a segment coordinate s∈{0,…,Nseg−1}s\in\{0,\dots,N_{\mathrm{seg}}-1\}. Define the reshape operator mat:ℂn→ℂm×Nseg\operatorname{mat}:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{m\times N_{\mathrm{seg}}} by

(mat⁡(𝐱))r,s=𝐱s​m+r,\bigl(\operatorname{mat}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)_{r,s}\;=\;\mathbf{x}_{s\,m+r},

and let vec:ℂm×Nseg→ℂn\operatorname{vec}:\mathbb{C}^{m\times N_{\mathrm{seg}}}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} be its inverse that stacks columns back into a length nn vector. Thus vec⁡(mat⁡(𝐱))=𝐱\operatorname{vec}(\operatorname{mat}(\mathbf{x}))=\mathbf{x} and mat⁡(vec⁡(𝐗))=𝐗\operatorname{mat}(\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf{X}))=\mathbf{X} for any 𝐗∈ℂm×Nseg\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times N_{\mathrm{seg}}}.

Ciphertext transformation operations. Following the transformation notation of Jiang et al. [34], for 𝐗∈ℂm×Nseg\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{C}^{m\times N_{\mathrm{seg}}} we define a segment shift ϕΔ\phi^{\Delta} and an intra-segment shift ψt\psi^{t} by

ϕΔ​(𝐗)r,s\displaystyle\phi^{\Delta}(\mathbf{X})_{r,s} =𝐗r,(s+Δ)modNseg,\displaystyle=\mathbf{X}_{r,\,(s+\Delta)\bmod N_{\mathrm{seg}}},
ψt​(𝐗)r,s\displaystyle\psi^{t}(\mathbf{X})_{r,s} =𝐗(r+t)modm,s.\displaystyle=\mathbf{X}_{(r+t)\bmod m,\,s}.

These shifts induce permutations on slot vectors,

ΦΔ​(𝐱)\displaystyle\Phi^{\Delta}(\mathbf{x}) =vec⁡(ϕΔ​(mat⁡(𝐱))),\displaystyle=\operatorname{vec}\!\bigl(\phi^{\Delta}(\operatorname{mat}(\mathbf{x}))\bigr),
Ψt​(𝐱)\displaystyle\Psi^{t}(\mathbf{x}) =vec⁡(ψt​(mat⁡(𝐱))).\displaystyle=\operatorname{vec}\!\bigl(\psi^{t}(\operatorname{mat}(\mathbf{x}))\bigr).

On ciphertexts, we apply the corresponding slot permutations and write ΦΔ​(⟨𝐱⟩)=⟨ΦΔ​(𝐱)⟩\Phi^{\Delta}(\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle)=\langle\Phi^{\Delta}(\mathbf{x})\rangle and Ψt​(⟨𝐱⟩)=⟨Ψt​(𝐱)⟩\Psi^{t}(\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle)=\langle\Psi^{t}(\mathbf{x})\rangle. Intuitively, ΦΔ\Phi^{\Delta} shifts by whole segments and can be realized as rot​(⟨𝐱⟩,Δ​m)\textsf{rot}(\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle;\Delta m), while Ψt\Psi^{t} shifts within each length mm segment. Concrete realizations can be found in Appendix A.1. When only the first C<NsegC<N_{\mathrm{seg}} segments are active and wrap-around is required within the active region, we use the restricted segment rotation ΦCΔ\Phi_{C}^{\Delta}, also detailed in Appendix A.1. When an object XX is represented by multiple ciphertext blocks, we write ⟨X⟩={⟨𝐱(ℓ)⟩}ℓ\langle X\rangle=\{\langle\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}\rangle\}_{\ell}. We overload ΦΔ​(⋅)\Phi^{\Delta}(\cdot) and Ψt​(⋅)\Psi^{t}(\cdot) to act elementwise on lists.

Minimal and expanded packings. Let xx be a real-valued vector with N⁡(x)N(x) logical scalar entries, where N⁡(x)N(x) excludes repetitions introduced for broadcasting, alignment, or interleaving. Under complex packing, each slot stores two independent real scalars, one in the real part and one in the imaginary part. The natural lower bound on ciphertext count is

Kmin​(x)=⌈N⁡(x)2​n⌉.K_{\min}(x)\;=\;\left\lceil\frac{N(x)}{2n}\right\rceil.

A packing of xx into KK ciphertexts is information-preserving if it stores all N⁡(x)N(x) entries without loss. A packing is minimal if it is information-preserving and attains K=Kmin​(x)K=K_{\min}(x), and expanded if it is information-preserving but uses K>Kmin​(x)K>K_{\min}(x). Figure 4 illustrates the distinction on an example.

III-A1 Stage Compatible Patterns

A hybrid FHE–MPC pipeline has two sources of avoidable overhead. First, adjacent FHE kernels may use incompatible packings, forcing an expensive ciphertext remap between them. Second, FHE–MPC boundaries may use more ciphertexts than necessary, inflating conversion communication. Stage Compatible Patterns address both problems through three rules applied to a canonical packing family ℱ={segment-column,folded-diagonal,head-major}\mathcal{F}=\{\text{segment-column},\allowbreak\ \text{folded-diagonal},\allowbreak\ \text{head-major}\}.

Each FHE kernel declares which format it accepts and which it produces. The three SCP rules are:

  1. 1.

    FHE→\toFHE. The producer outputs in the format the consumer expects, so no repacking is needed.

  2. 2.

    MPC→\toFHE. Data returning from MPC enters the next FHE kernel in minimal packing.

  3. 3.

    FHE→\toMPC. Data leaving an FHE kernel for MPC is exported in minimal packing.

Rule 1 eliminates FHE-side repacking. Rules 2 and 3 minimize the number of ciphertexts at each conversion boundary, directly reducing communication. The quantitative impact of Rules 2 and 3 on boundary cost is analyzed in Section V.

Proposition 1 (Stage Compatible Patterns).

Under the kernel interfaces of EncFormer, SCP achieves (i) zero FHE remap stages on all edges, and (ii) minimal ciphertext count KminK_{\min} at every FHE–MPC boundary. Violating Rule 1 on an FHE–FHE edge incurs Ω⁡(m​log⁡m)\Omega(m\log m) extra rotations per ciphertext [25]. Violating Rules 2 or 3 increases boundary conversion count beyond KminK_{\min}. The proof is in Appendix F.

III-B Plaintext–Ciphertext Projection Kernel

For plaintext–ciphertext multiplication, we use a shared kernel for linear projections Y=X​WY=XW, which instantiates a CKKS plaintext–ciphertext matrix multiplication under segment-column packing using standard baby-step-giant-step (BSGS) optimization [35, 8] and complex-packing optimizations [12].

Let X∈ℝm×dinX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{\mathrm{in}}} and W∈ℝdin×doutW\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times d_{\mathrm{out}}}. A CKKS ciphertext has nn slots, viewed as Nseg=n/mN_{\mathrm{seg}}=n/m contiguous segments of length mm via (mat⁡(𝐱))r,c=𝐱⁡[r+c​m]\bigl(\operatorname{mat}(\mathbf{x})\bigr)_{r,c}=\mathbf{x}[r+cm]. We activate the first C=cused≤NsegC=c_{\mathrm{used}}\leq N_{\mathrm{seg}} segments so one ciphertext packs CC columns. We group input channels into G=⌈din/C⌉G=\lceil d_{\mathrm{in}}/C\rceil ciphertexts and output channels into Bout=⌈dout/C⌉B_{\mathrm{out}}=\lceil d_{\mathrm{out}}/C\rceil ciphertexts.

For each g=0,…,G−1g=0,\dots,G-1, we encrypt ⟨𝐱(g)⟩\langle\mathbf{x}^{(g)}\rangle such that segment c∈{0,…,C−1}c\in\{0,\dots,C-1\} stores the length-mm column X[:,gC+c]X[:,\,gC+c]. For each b=0,…,Bout−1b=0,\dots,B_{\mathrm{out}}-1, the output ciphertext ⟨𝐲(b)⟩\langle\mathbf{y}^{(b)}\rangle stores columns Y[:,bC],…,Y[:,bC+C−1]Y[:,\,bC],\dots,Y[:,\,bC+C-1] in the same layout. Projection weights are encoded as CKKS plaintext vectors as detailed in Appendix A.2. We pre-permute plaintext weight columns so each projection emits the order consumed by its downstream kernel directly: QQ and KK use the score-friendly segment order, while VV uses the value-friendly head-major order.

Complex pairs compression. We pack two real input groups into one complex ciphertext by setting U=⌈G/2⌉U=\lceil G/2\rceil and, for each u∈0,…,U−1u\in{0,\dots,U-1}, defining the complexified input ⟨𝐱~(u)⟩\langle\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(u)}\rangle as

⟨𝐱~(u)⟩=⟨𝐱(2​u)+i​𝐱(2​u+1)⟩.\langle\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(u)}\rangle=\left\langle\mathbf{x}^{(2u)}+i\,\mathbf{x}^{(2u+1)}\right\rangle.

We call this packing operation complexification and call the reverse operation decomplexification.

BSGS optimization. Choose N1|CN_{1}\mid C and set N2=C/N1N_{2}=C/N_{1}. Let ΦC\Phi_{C} denote a segment cyclic shift within the first CC active segments. For each uu and q∈{0,…,N1−1}q\in\{0,\dots,N_{1}-1\} define ⟨𝐱~q(u)⟩=ΦCq​(⟨𝐱~(u)⟩)\langle\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(u)}_{q}\rangle=\Phi_{C}^{q}(\langle\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(u)}\rangle). For each output block bb and giant index p∈{0,…,N2−1}p\in\{0,\dots,N_{2}-1\} we accumulate a ciphertext

⟨𝐜~p(b)⟩=∑q=0N1−1∑u=0U−1(⟨𝐱~q(u)⟩⊙𝐰~u,p,q(b)),\langle\tilde{\mathbf{c}}^{(b)}_{p}\rangle=\sum_{q=0}^{N_{1}-1}\sum_{u=0}^{U-1}\left(\langle\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(u)}_{q}\rangle\odot\tilde{\mathbf{w}}^{(b)}_{u,p,q}\right),

We then decomplexify each giant-step accumulator by extracting its real part, and combine the N2N_{2} partial sums with segment shifts to obtain ⟨𝐲(b)⟩\langle\mathbf{y}^{(b)}\rangle:

⟨𝐜p(b)⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{c}^{(b)}_{p}\rangle =12​(⟨𝐜~p(b)⟩+conj​(⟨𝐜~p(b)⟩)),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl(\langle\tilde{\mathbf{c}}^{(b)}_{p}\rangle+\textsf{conj}(\langle\tilde{\mathbf{c}}^{(b)}_{p}\rangle)\Bigr),
⟨𝐲(b)⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{y}^{(b)}\rangle =∑p=0N2−1ΦCp​N1​(⟨𝐜p(b)⟩).\displaystyle=\sum_{p=0}^{N_{2}-1}\Phi_{C}^{pN_{1}}\!\left(\langle\mathbf{c}^{(b)}_{p}\rangle\right).

Appendix A.2 also describes an optional shortcut that fuses two projections that share the same input. The projection kernel satisfies SCP Rule 1 because it outputs in the segment-column packing consumed by the score kernel, and Rule 2 because MPC-produced inputs are imported into CKKS in minimal packing and consumed directly as {⟨𝐱(g)⟩}\{\langle\mathbf{x}^{(g)}\rangle\}.

III-C Ciphertext–Ciphertext Attention Kernels

Transformer attention is head-separable and exhibits a token-shift reuse pattern that we exploit to reduce key-switching operations relative to generic ciphertext–ciphertext matrix multiplication. For each head hh, we compute the score matrix S(h)=Q(h)​(K(h))⊤∈ℝm×mS^{(h)}=Q^{(h)}(K^{(h)})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} with a score kernel and the attention output O(h)=P(h)​V(h)∈ℝm×dhO^{(h)}=P^{(h)}V^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{h}} with a value kernel, where P(h)P^{(h)} is the post-softmax attention matrix.

Both kernels reuse the same small sets of segment shifts and intra-segment shifts on each ciphertext block, so we precompute rotation banks to avoid redundant key-switching operations. For block ℓ\ell with input ⟨𝐱(ℓ)⟩\langle\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}\rangle, let 𝒟,𝒯⊂ℤ\mathcal{D},\mathcal{T}\subset\mathbb{Z} be the required segment and intra-segment offsets. We precompute

𝖡𝖺𝗇𝗄Φ​(⟨𝐱(ℓ)⟩,𝒟)={Φδ​(⟨𝐱(ℓ)⟩)}δ∈𝒟,\mathsf{Bank}_{\Phi}\!\left(\langle\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}\rangle,\mathcal{D}\right)=\left\{\Phi^{\delta}\!\left(\langle\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}\rangle\right)\right\}_{\delta\in\mathcal{D}},
𝖡𝖺𝗇𝗄Ψ​(⟨𝐱(ℓ)⟩,𝒯)={Ψt​(⟨𝐱(ℓ)⟩)}t∈𝒯.\mathsf{Bank}_{\Psi}\!\left(\langle\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}\rangle,\mathcal{T}\right)=\left\{\Psi^{t}\!\left(\langle\mathbf{x}^{(\ell)}\rangle\right)\right\}_{t\in\mathcal{T}}.

When only the first C<NsegC<N_{\mathrm{seg}} segments are active, we use ΦCδ\Phi_{C}^{\delta} so that wrap-around stays within the active region. The inner loops then use bank lookups with ptmul, add, and ctmul, and all rotations occur only during bank construction.

III-C1 Score Kernel

Inputs are ⟨Q⟩\langle Q\rangle and ⟨K⟩\langle K\rangle in segment-column packing, where ⟨Q⟩={⟨𝐪(ℓ)⟩}ℓ\langle Q\rangle=\{\langle\mathbf{q}^{(\ell)}\rangle\}_{\ell} and ⟨K⟩={⟨𝐤(ℓ)⟩}ℓ\langle K\rangle=\{\langle\mathbf{k}^{(\ell)}\rangle\}_{\ell} encrypt QQ and KK. The output is a folded-diagonal ciphertext list {⟨𝐒t⟩}t=0m/2−1\{\langle\mathbf{S}_{t}\rangle\}_{t=0}^{m/2-1}. Folded-diagonal packing compresses two attention diagonals into one ciphertext: for each head hh, define the cyclic diagonal vector at offset Δ\Delta as

sΔh[j]=Sj,(j+Δ)modmh,j=0,…,m−1.s^{h}_{\Delta}[j]=S^{h}_{j,\,(j+\Delta)\bmod m},\quad j=0,\dots,m-1.

The offset pair (t,t+m/2)(t,t+m/2) is stored by placing their diagonals into the real and imaginary parts of a single vector:

vth[j]=sth[j]+ist+m/2h[j],t=0,…,m/2−1.v^{h}_{t}[j]=s^{h}_{t}[j]+i\,s^{h}_{t+m/2}[j],\quad t=0,\dots,m/2-1.

We assign one length-mm segment per head inside each ciphertext, with heads stacked across segments, and place different values of tt across ciphertext blocks. Figure 5 illustrates this layout in the kernel procedures.

Choose β|m\beta\mid m and set g=m/βg=m/\beta with gg even. We compute each folded-diagonal pair by reusing a fixed set of intra-segment shifts on QQ and KK. For each t∈{0,…,m/2−1}t\in\{0,\dots,m/2-1\}, write t=j⁡(t)​β+s⁡(t)t=j(t)\beta+s(t) with j⁡(t)=⌊t/β⌋j(t)=\lfloor t/\beta\rfloor and s⁡(t)=tmodβs(t)=t\bmod\beta. Pairing (t,t+m/2)(t,t+m/2) matches folded-diagonal packing, so each tt is produced by one complex multiply between a QQ shift and a complexified pair of KK shifts.

For each ciphertext block ℓ\ell, we precompute a QQ bank over the offsets

𝒯Q={0,−1,…,−(β−1)},\mathcal{T}_{Q}=\{0,-1,\dots,-(\beta-1)\},

where the negative shift aligns the QQ row index with the KK diagonal offset s⁡(t)s(t) in the inner product. We also precompute two KK banks over the offsets

𝒯K\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{K} ={jβ∣j=0,…,g/2−1},\displaystyle=\{j\beta\mid j=0,\dots,g/2-1\},
𝒯K,half\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{K,\mathrm{half}} ={m/2+jβ∣j=0,…,g/2−1}.\displaystyle=\{m/2+j\beta\mid j=0,\dots,g/2-1\}.

This yields

{⟨𝐪s(ℓ)⟩}s\displaystyle\{\langle\mathbf{q}^{(\ell)}_{s}\rangle\}_{s} :=𝖡𝖺𝗇𝗄Ψ​(⟨𝐪(ℓ)⟩,𝒯Q),\displaystyle:=\mathsf{Bank}_{\Psi}\bigl(\langle\mathbf{q}^{(\ell)}\rangle,\mathcal{T}_{Q}\bigr),
{⟨𝐤τ(ℓ)⟩}τ\displaystyle\{\langle\mathbf{k}^{(\ell)}_{\tau}\rangle\}_{\tau} :=𝖡𝖺𝗇𝗄Ψ​(⟨𝐤(ℓ)⟩,𝒯K∪𝒯K,half),\displaystyle:=\mathsf{Bank}_{\Psi}\bigl(\langle\mathbf{k}^{(\ell)}\rangle,\mathcal{T}_{K}\cup\mathcal{T}_{K,\mathrm{half}}\bigr),

Using these banks, we form one folded-diagonal pair per tt,

⟨𝐮t⟩=∑ℓ(⟨𝐪−s⁡(t)(ℓ)⟩⊙(⟨𝐤j⁡(t)​β(ℓ)⟩+i⁡⟨𝐤m/2+j⁡(t)​β(ℓ)⟩)).\langle\mathbf{u}_{t}\rangle=\sum_{\ell}\Bigl(\langle\mathbf{q}^{(\ell)}_{-s(t)}\rangle\odot\bigl(\langle\mathbf{k}^{(\ell)}_{j(t)\beta}\rangle+i\,\langle\mathbf{k}^{(\ell)}_{m/2+j(t)\beta}\rangle\bigr)\Bigr).

Finally, we aggregate the CC active segments into the first HH head segments and align the intra-segment offset. Let {𝐦c}c=0C−1\{\mathbf{m}_{c}\}_{c=0}^{C-1} be disjoint binary segment masks, where 𝐦c\mathbf{m}_{c} keeps exactly the cc-th active segment. This produces ⟨𝐒t⟩\langle\mathbf{S}_{t}\rangle in folded-diagonal packing,

⟨𝐒t⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{S}_{t}\rangle =Ψs⁡(t)​(∑c=0C−1Φ(cmodH)−c​(⟨𝐮t⟩⊙𝐦c)).\displaystyle=\Psi^{s(t)}\Biggl(\sum_{c=0}^{C-1}\Phi^{(c\bmod H)-c}\bigl(\langle\mathbf{u}_{t}\rangle\odot\mathbf{m}_{c}\bigr)\Biggr).

When C≢0(modH)C\not\equiv 0\pmod{H}, different ciphertext blocks start at different head-phase offsets, requiring a block-dependent phase correction before combining. Mask construction and the full phase-correction procedure are given in Appendix A.3; the equations above describe the core accumulation without this correction for clarity.

III-C2 Value Kernel

Let HblkH_{\mathrm{blk}} be the number of heads packed in one value ciphertext block and let BV=⌈H/Hblk⌉B_{V}=\lceil H/H_{\mathrm{blk}}\rceil. The CKKS inputs are the folded-diagonal softmax ciphertext list

⟨Pfd⟩={⟨𝐩fd(ℓ)⟩}ℓ=0BV−1\langle P_{\mathrm{fd}}\rangle=\{\langle\mathbf{p}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{fd}}\rangle\}_{\ell=0}^{B_{V}-1}

and the value ciphertext list

⟨V⟩={⟨𝐯(ℓ)⟩}ℓ=0BV−1.\langle V\rangle=\{\langle\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}\rangle\}_{\ell=0}^{B_{V}-1}.

Each value ciphertext ⟨𝐯(ℓ)⟩\langle\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}\rangle uses head-major packing: segment k⁡(h~,u)=h~​dh+uk(\tilde{h},u)=\tilde{h}\,d_{h}+u stores V(ℓ,h~)[:,u]∈ℝmV^{(\ell,\tilde{h})}[:,u]\in\mathbb{R}^{m} for h~∈{0,…,Hblk−1}\tilde{h}\in\{0,\dots,H_{\mathrm{blk}}-1\} and u∈{0,…,dh−1}u\in\{0,\dots,d_{h}-1\}. Thus, the dhd_{h} channels of each local head are contiguous, and different heads occupy disjoint blocks of dhd_{h} segments. The output is the head-major ciphertext list

⟨Ohm⟩={⟨𝐨hm(ℓ)⟩}ℓ=0BV−1\langle O_{\mathrm{hm}}\rangle=\{\langle\mathbf{o}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{hm}}\rangle\}_{\ell=0}^{B_{V}-1}

which encodes O=P​V∈ℝm×dO=PV\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}. The subsequent output projection absorbs the head-major-to-segment-column conversion by pre-permuting its plaintext weight columns, as detailed in Appendix A.2, so no explicit FHE remap is needed.

For each block ℓ\ell, we reuse two banks. First, we complexify the value block and build a Ψ\Psi bank over token offsets:

⟨𝐮(ℓ)⟩\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{u}^{(\ell)}\rangle =⟨𝐯(ℓ)⟩−i​Ψm/2​(⟨𝐯(ℓ)⟩),\displaystyle=\langle\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}\rangle-i\,\Psi^{m/2}\!\bigl(\langle\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}\rangle\bigr),
{⟨𝐮t(ℓ)⟩}t=0m/2−1\displaystyle\{\langle\mathbf{u}^{(\ell)}_{t}\rangle\}_{t=0}^{m/2-1} =𝖡𝖺𝗇𝗄Ψ​(⟨𝐮(ℓ)⟩,{0,…,m/2−1}).\displaystyle=\mathsf{Bank}_{\Psi}\bigl(\langle\mathbf{u}^{(\ell)}\rangle,\{0,\dots,m/2-1\}\bigr).

Second, let 𝐧u\mathbf{n}_{u} be the binary segment mask that keeps exactly channel offset uu across the HblkH_{\mathrm{blk}} local heads in one block (Appendix A.3). For each t∈{0,…,m/2−1}t\in\{0,\dots,m/2-1\}, we align and broadcast the folded-diagonal weights by

⟨𝐛t(ℓ)⟩=∑u=0dh−1(Φt−u​(⟨𝐩fd(ℓ)⟩)⊙𝐧u).\langle\mathbf{b}^{(\ell)}_{t}\rangle=\sum_{u=0}^{d_{h}-1}\left(\Phi^{t-u}\!\bigl(\langle\mathbf{p}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{fd}}\rangle\bigr)\odot\mathbf{n}_{u}\right).

The block output is then

⟨𝐨hm(ℓ)⟩=∑t=0m/2−1(⟨𝐮t(ℓ)⟩⊙⟨𝐛t(ℓ)⟩),ℓ=0,…,BV−1.\langle\mathbf{o}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{hm}}\rangle=\sum_{t=0}^{m/2-1}\bigl(\langle\mathbf{u}^{(\ell)}_{t}\rangle\odot\langle\mathbf{b}^{(\ell)}_{t}\rangle\bigr),\qquad\ell=0,\dots,B_{V}-1.

Each ⟨𝐨hm(ℓ)⟩\langle\mathbf{o}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{hm}}\rangle remains in head-major layout, and the output projection consumes this list directly via plaintext weight pre-permutation.

Putting it together. The score kernel consumes the segment-column packed QQ and KK from the projection kernel (SCP Rule 1) and exports the scores into Kmin​(S)=⌈H​m2/(2​n)⌉K_{\min}(S)=\lceil Hm^{2}/(2n)\rceil ciphertexts in minimal folded-diagonal packing at the FHE–MPC boundary (Rule 3). The internal per-tt representation {⟨𝐒t⟩}\{\langle\mathbf{S}_{t}\rangle\} is repacked into a sequential minimal stream before conversion; see Appendix A.3. The MPC softmax block receives this stream, converts it to additive shares via the CKKS-to-MPC protocol, evaluates the MBMax softmax surrogate securely, and converts the result back to CKKS in minimal folded-diagonal packing (Kmin​(P)=⌈H​m2/(2​n)⌉K_{\min}(P)=\lceil Hm^{2}/(2n)\rceil ciphertexts, Rule 2). The value kernel then combines the folded-diagonal softmax list ⟨Pfd⟩\langle P_{\mathrm{fd}}\rangle with the head-major value list {⟨𝐯(ℓ)⟩}ℓ\{\langle\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}\rangle\}_{\ell} without FHE-side repacking, and outputs ⟨Ohm⟩\langle O_{\mathrm{hm}}\rangle, which the output projection consumes directly through pre-permuted weight columns (Rule 1). This keeps the MPC–FHE boundary at minimal ciphertext count while moving the broadcast into the FHE kernel where it composes cleanly with the value layout. Figure 5 illustrates both attention kernels on a toy instance. The top row shows the score kernel producing folded-diagonal score ciphertexts {⟨𝐒t⟩}\{\langle\mathbf{S}_{t}\rangle\} that are exported to MPC for softmax, and the bottom row shows the value kernel consuming the folded-diagonal softmax ciphertext list ⟨Pfd⟩\langle P_{\mathrm{fd}}\rangle together with the head-major value ciphertext list {⟨𝐯(ℓ)⟩}ℓ\{\langle\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}\rangle\}_{\ell} to output the head-major ciphertext list ⟨Ohm⟩\langle O_{\mathrm{hm}}\rangle encoding O=P​VO=PV.

Table II reports the key-switching counts of our attention kernels for BERT-base and compares them against prior work. The EncFormer counts are measured from the implementation; the BOLT, Powerformer, and BLB counts are analytically derived from their published algorithms under the same tensor shapes (m=128m=128, d=768d=768, H=12H=12, n=16384n=16384). Rather than summing rotations and ciphertext multiplications directly, the table also reports a weighted primitive-cost proxy in seconds using measured PhantomFHE A100 primitive latencies (trot=2.32t_{\mathrm{rot}}=2.32 ms, tctmul=2.65t_{\mathrm{ctmul}}=2.65 ms; Section VII-C). Appendix A.3 provides the asymptotic derivations.

IV Communication-Efficient MPC Blocks

IV-A MPC Fixed-point Primitives

All MPC computation uses fixed-point arithmetic over ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}} with additive shares [[⋅]]2ℓ[[\cdot]]_{2^{\ell}}. Real values are encoded with public fractional precision FF as ⌊r⋅2F⌉∈ℤ2ℓ\lfloor r\cdot 2^{F}\rceil\in\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}}, and all public constants and polynomial coefficients use the same scale. Table III summarizes the MPC primitives used throughout. We denote secure fixed-point multiplication by Π×\Pi_{\times}, with truncation back to scale 2F2^{F}.

IV-B Protocols for Non-linear Layers

The nonlinear approximation functions for Softmax and LayerNorm follow Powerformer [12], and the GELU piecewise approximation follows BOLT [8]. Our contribution is the MPC protocol realization of these approximations. By expressing the batch nonlinearities as short chains of MPC primitives, EncFormer uses 7 interactive MPC rounds per layer: 3 for MBMax (Softmax), 4 for GELU, and 0 for MBLN, since it reduces to local operations on additive shares. Appendix E compares these counts against prior systems.

IV-B1 MPC MBMax Protocol

We replace Softmax with the Batch Power-Max approximation from Powerformer using a power map and a fixed public normalizer. A single public constant RdR_{d} is distilled offline and reused during inference together with the public shift cc and exponent p=5p=5. The approximation is

𝐘=(𝐗+c)pRd,p=5,\mathbf{Y}\;=\;\frac{(\mathbf{X}+c)^{p}}{R_{d}},\qquad p=5, (1)

applied elementwise. Algorithm 1 realizes MBMax as a secure MPC protocol using a short multiplication chain and a final multiplication by the public fixed point constant 1/Rd1/R_{d}.

IV-B2 MPC MBLN Protocol

We adopt the Batch LayerNorm approximation from Powerformer, which replaces variance-dependent normalization with a fixed public scale. For a row x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

y=γ⊙x−μl⋅Rd+β,μ=RowMean⁡(x).y\;=\;\gamma\odot\frac{x-\mu}{l\cdot R_{d}}+\beta,\qquad\mu=\mathrm{RowMean}(x). (2)

We fold the constant scale into γ~=γ/(l⋅Rd)\tilde{\gamma}=\gamma/(l\cdot R_{d}) so that MBLN reduces to computing the row mean, centering the row, and applying a public elementwise affine map, which Algorithm 2 realizes as a secure MPC protocol.

IV-B3 GELU

We evaluate GELU using the piecewise approximation and secure selection protocol from BOLT [8], following the standard hybrid split used by BLB [10]. Concretely, CKKS forms the two candidate ciphertexts F0​(𝐱)F_{0}(\mathbf{x}) and F1​(𝐱)F_{1}(\mathbf{x}), and MPC selects among {0,F0​(𝐱),F1​(𝐱),𝐱}\{0,F_{0}(\mathbf{x}),F_{1}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{x}\} using Πcmp\Pi_{\mathrm{cmp}} and Πmux\Pi_{\mathrm{mux}}. This requires converting both F0​(𝐱)F_{0}(\mathbf{x}) and F1​(𝐱)F_{1}(\mathbf{x}), which increases the inbound conversion count for the GELU block; full protocol details are given in Appendix B.

V Boundary Co-Design and Secure Conversion

In EncFormer, boundary design is part of the system architecture rather than a post-processing detail. We therefore pair a cost model for boundary placement with a secure complex CKKS–MPC conversion protocol that reduces payload while preserving compatibility with real-valued MPC blocks.

V-A Cost Model for Boundary Design

Conversion overhead grows with the number of CKKS–MPC conversion pairs and with the total ciphertext payload converted at the FHE–MPC boundaries. Both factors depend on the boundary packing and on CKKS parameters that determine the ciphertext size.

Fix a hybrid inference decomposition with RR MPC blocks indexed by r=1,…,Rr=1,\dots,R. Block rr consumes a complex-valued boundary tensor xr→x^{\rightarrow}_{r} and produces a complex-valued boundary tensor xr←x^{\leftarrow}_{r}. A hybrid design chooses a packing for every xr→x^{\rightarrow}_{r} and xr←x^{\leftarrow}_{r} and specifies where conversions occur.

V-A1 Baseline Conversions and Decision Rule

We define the minimal-conversion baseline design BB by two properties. First, BB performs exactly one entry conversion CKKS→\toMPC and one exit conversion MPC→\toCKKS for each MPC block, and performs no other conversions. Therefore, BB uses exactly RR conversion pairs, which is the minimum possible for a fixed set of RR MPC blocks. Second, BB uses minimal packing, defined in Section III-A, at every boundary tensor so that each xr→x^{\rightarrow}_{r} and xr←x^{\leftarrow}_{r} is represented using exactly Kmin​(x)K_{\min}(x) ciphertexts. In a standard Transformer encoder layer, the nonlinearities consist of the attention softmax, two layer normalizations, and the feed-forward GELU activation (Figure 1). Accordingly, we decompose each layer into R=4R=4 MPC blocks (Softmax, LN1, GELU, LN2), so the baseline uses exactly four FHE↔\leftrightarrowMPC conversion pairs per layer.

However, deviating from BB can still be beneficial because expanded packings or additional conversions can reduce CKKS-side or MPC-side work by enabling layouts and kernels with fewer key-switched operations. These choices increase conversion overhead by increasing either the number of conversion pairs or the number of ciphertexts converted. Prior works do not provide an analytic criterion for when a non-minimal conversion strategy is worthwhile. We model this trade-off explicitly and use it to decide when moving away from BB is worthwhile. Figure 6 summarizes the design space.

We write end-to-end latency as

Ttotal=Tconv+Tckks+Tmpc.T_{\text{total}}\;=\;T_{\text{conv}}\;+\;T_{\text{ckks}}\;+\;T_{\text{mpc}}. (3)

We treat TconvT_{\text{conv}} as the aggregate boundary-conversion latency induced by the chosen conversion placement and boundary packing. Thus Tconv​(D)T_{\text{conv}}(D) captures both the number of conversion pairs in design DD and the total ciphertext payload converted at the boundaries.

Let BB denote the minimal-conversion baseline and DD a candidate design. Define

Δ​Tconv\displaystyle\Delta T_{\text{conv}} =Tconv​(D)−Tconv​(B),\displaystyle=T_{\text{conv}}(D)-T_{\text{conv}}(B),
Δ​Tcomp\displaystyle\Delta T_{\text{comp}} =(Tckks​(D)+Tmpc​(D))\displaystyle=\bigl(T_{\text{ckks}}(D)+T_{\text{mpc}}(D)\bigr)
−(Tckks​(B)+Tmpc​(B)).\displaystyle}{\displaystyle-\bigl(T_{\text{ckks}}(B)+T_{\text{mpc}}(B)\bigr).

We prefer DD if

Δ​Tconv+Δ​Tcomp< 0.\Delta T_{\text{conv}}\;+\;\Delta T_{\text{comp}}\;<\;0. (4)

This condition states that any increase in conversion overhead under DD is acceptable only when it is more than offset by a reduction in CKKS-side and MPC-side latency, resulting in a net decrease in end-to-end latency.

V-A2 Parameterization

We parameterize Δ​Tconv\Delta T_{\text{conv}} and Δ​Tcomp\Delta T_{\text{comp}} in terms of CKKS parameters, network profile, the total CKKS compute time difference Δ​Tckks=Tckks​(B)−Tckks​(D)\Delta T_{\text{ckks}}=T_{\text{ckks}}(B)-T_{\text{ckks}}(D), and MPC round savings. Let KextraK_{\text{extra}} denote the additional ciphertexts converted beyond the baseline, RextraR_{\text{extra}} the additional conversion round-trips, ct​_​bytes​(N,L)=2​N​L⋅8\mathrm{ct\_bytes}(N,L)=2NL\cdot 8 the serialized ciphertext size for ring degree NN with LL RNS limbs, and BW\mathrm{BW}, RTT\mathrm{RTT} the network bandwidth and round-trip time. Then

Δ​Tconv=Kextra⋅ct​_​bytes​(N,L)BW+Rextra⋅RTT,\Delta T_{\text{conv}}=\frac{K_{\text{extra}}\cdot\mathrm{ct\_bytes}(N,L)}{\mathrm{BW}}+R_{\text{extra}}\cdot\mathrm{RTT}, (5)
Δ​Tcomp≈−(Δ​Tckks+Rsaved⋅(RTT+Cround/BW)),\Delta T_{\text{comp}}\approx-\bigl(\Delta T_{\text{ckks}}+R_{\text{saved}}\cdot({\mathrm{RTT}}+C_{\text{round}}/\mathrm{BW})\bigr), (6)

where Δ​Tckks\Delta T_{\text{ckks}} is the total CKKS compute time saved by DD relative to BB (positive when DD reduces FHE work), RsavedR_{\text{saved}} is the number of MPC rounds saved, and CroundC_{\text{round}} is the MPC communication per round in bytes. The per-round communication depends on the MPC backend: for Beaver-triple multiplication on EE elements with ring bit-width ℓ\ell, Cround=E⋅4​⌈ℓ/8⌉C_{\text{round}}=E\cdot 4\lceil\ell/8\rceil.

Eqs. (5)–(6) can be used to estimate the sign of Δ​Tconv+Δ​Tcomp\Delta T_{\text{conv}}+\Delta T_{\text{comp}} and guide boundary placement. We treat them as a screening tool rather than a precise predictor, since Δ​Tckks\Delta T_{\text{ckks}} and CroundC_{\text{round}} are measured under specific deployment conditions. Appendices D and H provide further discussion and validation details.

V-B Complex Conversion Protocol

Prior CKKS–MPC conversions in hybrid systems [36, 10] use only the real part of each CKKS ciphertext, leaving the imaginary part unused.

At an FHE–MPC boundary, we convert between a CKKS ciphertext ⟨𝐦⟩\langle\mathbf{m}\rangle at scale Δ\Delta and MPC additive shares over ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}}. We represent boundary values in a fixed point so that decryption and decoding yield a slot vector 𝐱+i​𝐲∈ℂn\mathbf{x}+i\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{C}^{n} where 𝐱,𝐲∈ℤn\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} fit in the signed range of ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}}. Following BLB [10], we sample randomness directly in the polynomial ring modulo the coefficient modulus and then apply the CKKS encoding map, rather than sampling real numbers and encoding them. We write AN,q2A_{N,q}^{2} for the CKKS ciphertext space with ring degree NN and modulus qq and we set q=Qconvq=Q_{\mathrm{conv}} at the boundary.

V-B1 Complex CKKS-to-MPC Conversion

Let QconvQ_{\mathrm{conv}} be the ciphertext modulus at the boundary. Given ⟨𝐦⟩\langle\mathbf{m}\rangle from P1P_{1} that encrypts an encoding of 𝐱+i​𝐲\mathbf{x}+i\mathbf{y}, the conversion outputs ring shares [[𝐱]]2ℓ[[\mathbf{x}]]_{2^{\ell}} and [[𝐲]]2ℓ[[\mathbf{y}]]_{2^{\ell}}. P1P_{1} masks the boundary plaintext by sampling a uniform 𝐫^←RQconv\hat{\mathbf{r}}\leftarrow R_{Q_{\mathrm{conv}}} and sending ⟨𝐦⟩+𝐫^\langle\mathbf{m}\rangle+\hat{\mathbf{r}} for decryption, so P0P_{0} decrypts a uniformly masked plaintext-ring element. Protocol ΠC2Mℂ\Pi_{\mathrm{C2M}}^{\mathbb{C}} in Algorithm 3 realizes this conversion.

The two plaintext shares in Steps 1 and 2 reconstruct the unmasked boundary plaintext modulo QconvQ_{\mathrm{conv}} because (𝐩^+𝐫^)+(−𝐫^)≡𝐩^(\hat{\mathbf{p}}+\hat{\mathbf{r}})+(-\hat{\mathbf{r}})\equiv\hat{\mathbf{p}} where 𝐩^=Encode⁡(𝐱+i​𝐲,Δ)\hat{\mathbf{p}}=\mathrm{Encode}(\mathbf{x}+i\mathbf{y},\Delta). By correctness of ΠField2Ring\Pi_{\mathrm{Field2Ring}} in Appendix C, Step 3 preserves the same signed fixed point plaintext in ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}} except with negligible statistical error. CKKS decoding is a linear map from the plaintext ring to the slot space, so decoding each additive plaintext share locally in Step 4 yields additive shares of the decoded vector. Therefore, the outputs reconstruct 𝐱+i​𝐲\mathbf{x}+i\mathbf{y} up to the standard CKKS decoding error. If the per-slot decoding error is below 1/21/2 in both real and imaginary parts at the boundary scale, rounding recovers the intended integers in ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}}. We empirically verify this condition on PhantomFHE (n=214n=2^{14}, scale Δ=240\Delta=2^{40}, 40-bit body primes): the maximum per-slot absolute error after one encrypt–decode round-trip is ∼9×10−6{\sim}9\times 10^{-6}, well below 1/21/2.

V-B2 Complex MPC-to-CKKS Conversion

Given ring shares [[𝐱]]2ℓ[[\mathbf{x}]]_{2^{\ell}} and [[𝐲]]2ℓ[[\mathbf{y}]]_{2^{\ell}}, the conversion outputs a CKKS ciphertext ⟨𝐦⟩\langle\mathbf{m}\rangle at scale Δ\Delta that decrypts and decodes to a value close to 𝐱+i​𝐲\mathbf{x}+i\mathbf{y}. We mirror prior real-only conversions by locally encoding the two share vectors as plaintext ring shares and then switching these plaintext shares from ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}} to ℤQconv\mathbb{Z}_{Q_{\mathrm{conv}}} using ΠRing2Field\Pi_{\mathrm{Ring2Field}}. Protocol ΠM2Cℂ\Pi_{\mathrm{M2C}}^{\mathbb{C}} in Algorithm 4 realizes this conversion by encrypting one plaintext share and adding the other plaintext share locally.

By construction, the two encoded plaintext shares in Step 1 add to an encoding of 𝐱+i​𝐲\mathbf{x}+i\mathbf{y} under the signed fixed point interpretation in ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}}. By correctness of ΠRing2Field\Pi_{\mathrm{Ring2Field}} in Appendix C, Step 2 converts these plaintext shares to RQconvR_{Q_{\mathrm{conv}}} while preserving their sum modulo QconvQ_{\mathrm{conv}} except with negligible statistical error. After Step 4, the ciphertext encrypts the sum of the two plaintext shares, so decryption and decoding recover 𝐱+i​𝐲\mathbf{x}+i\mathbf{y} up to the standard CKKS decoding error. If the per-slot decoding error is below 1/21/2 in both parts at the boundary scale, a subsequent CKKS-to-MPC conversion recovers the intended integers in ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}} under rounding.

V-B3 Security of Complex Conversion

We consider semi-honest adversaries. In ΠC2Mℂ\Pi_{\mathrm{C2M}}^{\mathbb{C}}, P0P_{0} receives a masked ciphertext and decrypts a plaintext that is uniform in RQconvR_{Q_{\mathrm{conv}}} because 𝐫^\hat{\mathbf{r}} is uniform and unknown to P0P_{0}, so the decryption result is statistically independent of the encoded message. In ΠM2Cℂ\Pi_{\mathrm{M2C}}^{\mathbb{C}}, P1P_{1} receives only a CKKS ciphertext encrypting P0P_{0}’s plaintext share, which reveals no information by semantic security, and then adds its own plaintext share locally. By composition, if ΠField2Ring\Pi_{\mathrm{Field2Ring}} and ΠRing2Field\Pi_{\mathrm{Ring2Field}} are secure, then the conversion protocols leak nothing beyond their prescribed outputs and public parameters.

V-B4 Communication Overhead and Compatibility

A CKKS ciphertext has nn complex slots, corresponding to 2​n2n real values across the real and imaginary parts. A real-only conversion exports a single part and therefore transmits one ciphertext per real vector per direction. Our complex conversion exports both parts so one ciphertext carries two independent real vectors, reducing the number of ciphertexts transmitted per direction from kk to ⌈k/2⌉\lceil k/2\rceil for kk real vectors. The conversion outputs two real share vectors, so existing MPC protocols for real-valued nonlinearities apply by processing the two parts independently. For pipelines that otherwise treat CKKS ciphertexts as real, boundary-level complexify/decomplexify wrappers convert two real ciphertexts into one complex ciphertext and back. Section VII-A shows that their overhead is small relative to the communication savings.

Table IV compares analytically derived ciphertext counts per MPC block for the theoretical minimal baseline, prior hybrid systems, and EncFormer. Prior papers do not report boundary payload in bytes, so we compare at the level of ciphertext counts under a common tensor shape and slot budget. Overall, EncFormer reduces conversion ciphertext count by 25% relative to BOLT and by 57% relative to BLB, while still allowing an intentionally expanded GELU boundary when the PhantomFHE decision rule predicts a net latency win.

Relationship to Complex FHE Packing. BOLT and BLB use real-only conversion at FHE–MPC boundaries, transmitting one ciphertext per real vector [8, 10]. Powerformer uses complex packing inside its FHE kernels to halve key-switching counts via a generic blockwise CCMM [12, 34], but its output remains in column packing throughout.

EncFormer differs in two ways. First, the attention kernels are not generic CCMM reductions but exploit the diagonal structure of Q​K⊤QK^{\top} and the token-shift structure of P​VPV to produce specialized folded-diagonal and head-major output formats that chain across stages via SCP without repacking. Second, EncFormer uses complex packing at FHE–MPC boundaries, packing two real boundary tensors into one complex ciphertext and halving conversion payload. This boundary-level use is absent from Powerformer’s FHE-only pipeline.

Modulus Trimming Optimization. CKKS-to-MPC conversion payload depends on the serialized ciphertext size, which scales with the remaining modulus chain. Ciphertexts should arrive at the boundary at the shortest admissible modulus level, since no further CKKS multiplications are needed. If a ciphertext reaches the boundary at a higher level, P1P_{1} can modulus switch it down before running ΠC2Mℂ\Pi_{\mathrm{C2M}}^{\mathbb{C}} to reduce transmitted payload and improve TconvT_{\mathrm{conv}} in Eq. (3). This optimization applies only to CKKS-to-MPC conversion since MPC-to-CKKS outputs must retain sufficient modulus for subsequent CKKS evaluation.

Let LconvL_{\mathrm{conv}} be the target conversion level and set q=QLconvq=Q_{L_{\mathrm{conv}}}. We choose LconvL_{\mathrm{conv}} as the smallest level that keeps conversion statistically safe:

log2⁡(q)≥ℓ+σ+1andq/2>Δ⋅Bmax.\log_{2}(q)\geq\ell+\sigma+1\qquad\text{and}\qquad q/2>\Delta\cdot B_{\max}.

P1P_{1} repeatedly applies ModSwitchToNext\mathrm{ModSwitchToNext} (which removes the last RNS prime without rescaling) until reaching LconvL_{\mathrm{conv}}, then runs ΠC2Mℂ\Pi_{\mathrm{C2M}}^{\mathbb{C}} unchanged. This reduces only the transmission size; the MPC ring size and ring-to-field conversion cost are unaffected.

VI Experimental Setup

We implement the main EncFormer pipeline with PhantomFHE for CKKS and EzPC/SCI [37, 38] for MPC. The supporting matched-backend comparison uses Liberate.FHE and CrypTen [39]. All FHE kernels run on NVIDIA A100 GPUs. MPC values use fixed-point encoding with F=13F=13 fractional bits over ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}} with ℓ=43\ell=43. Table V lists the CKKS parameters per FHE block, chosen so that the modulus chain is close to minimal at each conversion boundary.

Following [8, 16, 10], we evaluate GPT2-base, BERT-base, and BERT-large. For accuracy, we use the GLUE tasks MRPC, RTE, and SST-2 [40]. We start from public Hugging Face checkpoints [41], fine-tune them following Powerformer-style training, and distill surrogate parameters for encrypted inference; training details are given in Appendix J.

Unless otherwise specified, we report four standard network profiles: LAN at 1 Gbps with 0.3 ms RTT, WAN1 at 400 Mbps with 4 ms RTT, WAN2 at 100 Mbps with 4 ms RTT, and WAN3 at 100 Mbps with 80 ms RTT.

Latency Methodology. All FHE kernel and MPC local computation times are measured on a single A100 GPU, reported as the mean of three independent trials after one warm-up iteration. LAN and WAN latencies are computed by adding measured local compute time to a network overlay derived from measured byte counts and round counts under each profile, following the same methodology as prior work [8, 10, 16].

Baseline Sources. The baseline metrics for prior systems are taken from the corresponding papers under their stated experimental settings [8, 16, 10, 11, 12]. When a paper does not directly report a particular aggregate but provides a complete protocol specification, we derive the missing quantity by counting operations under the same tensor shapes. For example, the BOLT and BLB entries in Table IV are obtained by analyzing their reported MPC protocols and boundary ciphertext dimensions.

VII Evaluation

VII-A Microbenchmarks

VII-A1 FHE Library Comparison

To contextualize the runtimes reported in Section VII-B, we benchmark the two GPU CKKS backends used in this paper, PhantomFHE [20] and Liberate.FHE [21], under a common parameter set. Table VI reports the latency of core CKKS primitives, where PhantomFHE is on average about an order of magnitude faster than Liberate.FHE, consistent with prior library comparisons [42]. PhantomFHE does not support bootstrapping, while Liberate.FHE does, which is why FHE-only baselines that require bootstrapping are evaluated under Liberate.FHE in Table X.

VII-A2 Multiplicative Depth Sensitivity

Figure 7 shows that CKKS primitive latency increases with multiplicative depth for both libraries, with higher and more variable latency for Liberate.FHE. This supports our design choice to keep FHE depth low and refresh via FHE–MPC conversions.

VII-A3 Conversion Protocol Comparison

We benchmark CKKS–MPC conversion for two real-valued ciphertexts under four standard network profiles. The real baseline protocol [36, 8, 10] converts the ciphertexts independently and transmits two ciphertexts per direction. Our complex variant packs the two vectors into the real and imaginary parts of one ciphertext and transmits one ciphertext per direction. We report end-to-end conversion latency, including CKKS-side complexification and decomplexification overhead, and network delay. The total payload per conversion pair is 20.97 MB for Real, 10.49 MB for Complex, and 6.41 MB for Complex plus trimming. Table VII reports latency and speedup across networks.

The nearly 2×2\times reduction confirms that the complex protocol halves boundary communication, while trimming provides additional gain when the ciphertext reaches the boundary with excess modulus.

VII-B End-to-end Evaluation

VII-B1 Latency and Communication

Our main evaluation uses the PhantomFHE+EzPC pipeline and reports end-to-end latency together with online MPC communication. Section VII-C compares the hybrid and FHE-only paradigms under a matched backend.

Following prior work [8, 16, 10], the Comm column reports only the online communication of the interactive MBMax and GELU protocols, excluding FHE–MPC conversion payload. We report boundary-conversion effects separately through Table IV; the latency columns include all costs, including conversion. The total communication including conversion payload is approximately 1.1×1.1\times the online-only figure for EncFormer under BERT-base; comparable multipliers apply to the baselines, as detailed in Appendix H. The relative ranking is preserved under total communication.

EncFormer achieves the lowest latency and online MPC communication across all three models. Relative to BLB, EncFormer is 1.3×\times faster on average while sending 1.4×\times less online MPC traffic. Relative to BumbleBee and BOLT, the corresponding average latency and communication gains are 2.1×\times/2.6×\times and 9.8×\times/30.4×\times, respectively. Section VII-C provides a matched-backend comparison that controls for library differences.

For context, plaintext inference on a single A100 GPU takes approximately 4.5 ms for BERT-base, 9.1 ms for BERT-large, and 4.2 ms for GPT2-base. The secure pipeline is roughly 3×1043{\times}10^{4} slower, which is consistent with the overhead reported by prior hybrid systems [8, 16, 10].

VII-B2 Accuracy

Table IX compares encrypted inference against a public uncased baseline (standard BERT with exact softmax, LayerNorm, and GELU) and a fine-tuned teacher that uses the same MBMax, MBLN, and approximate GELU surrogates as the encrypted pipeline. The uncased baseline is higher because it uses exact nonlinearities. The small gap of 0.25–0.35% between the teacher and EncFormer shows that the FHE+MPC execution itself introduces minimal quality loss, and that the remaining accuracy drop is due to the surrogate approximations, not the encrypted computation.

VII-C Hybrid vs. FHE-Only Paradigm Comparison

A natural question is whether the hybrid FHE–MPC approach is worthwhile compared to FHE-only pipelines that avoid interaction entirely. To answer this, we implement EncFormer with Liberate.FHE and CrypTen so that the comparison uses the same FHE backend and nonlinear approximations as the FHE-only baselines THOR and Powerformer.

Table X shows the layer-wise breakdown. FHE-only systems offer a cleaner non-interactive solution with no communication during inference. However, if the deployment permits lightweight client–server interaction, the hybrid approach is substantially more efficient. Under LAN, eliminating bootstrapping yields a 3.5×\times speedup over THOR and 1.9×\times over Powerformer. The advantage narrows under WAN as MPC round-trip costs grow, so practitioners should choose based on their network conditions.

Even comparing only FHE linear components, EncFormer is faster. For BERT-base, the FHE linear time per layer is 172.6 s for EncFormer versus 229.4 s for THOR and 230.9 s for Powerformer, thanks to SCP eliminating repacking and shallower depth reducing per-operation cost, as shown in Figure 7.

VII-D Ablation Studies

VII-D1 GELU Conversion Cost Analysis

We study the inbound CKKS–MPC boundary of the GELU block and compare two pipeline variants that differ only in where the GELU polynomials are evaluated. In the minimal baseline, the pipeline converts only the GELU input tensor 𝐱\mathbf{x} into MPC using minimal packing, evaluates the polynomial candidates in MPC, and then applies cmp\mathrm{cmp} and mux\mathrm{mux}. In EncFormer’s CKKS pre-evaluation variant, we evaluate the polynomial candidates, F0​(𝐱)F_{0}(\mathbf{x}) and F1​(𝐱)F_{1}(\mathbf{x}), in CKKS and convert 𝐱\mathbf{x} together with the candidates into MPC, so that MPC performs only cmp\mathrm{cmp} and mux\mathrm{mux}. Appendix B describes the details of the two versions of GELU protocol adopted by EncFormer.

Figure 8 reports the end-to-end latency difference between CKKS pre-evaluation and the baseline for BERT-base and BERT-large, decomposed into the added conversion overhead and the computation change under our cost model. With PhantomFHE, the MPC cost reduction dominates on WAN1–WAN3, making CKKS pre-evaluation preferable under the decision rule in Eq. (4), while the net change on LAN is small, we use expanded packing for our main implementation pipeline. With the alternative Liberate.FHE implementation, however, CKKS pre-evaluation incurs substantially higher CKKS-side cost, so the net improvement is no longer robust across network profiles. Since the deployment network may be unknown a priori, we therefore adopt the no CKKS pre-evaluation GELU split for the results in Table X.

VII-D2 Contribution of Each Optimization

Table XI compares EncFormer against BLB and two internal variants. In w/o CC, we disable complex conversion and remove GELU pre-evaluation. In w/o SCP, we keep the same kernels but force additional repacking between FHE stages. The comparison shows that EncFormer’s gains come from lower online MPC traffic, fewer interactive rounds, and the elimination of cross-stage FHE remaps.

Without SCP, ciphertext repacking is needed at three direct FHE–FHE edges per layer: QKV→\toScore, QKV→\toValue, and Value→\toOUT. Each edge remaps BB ciphertext blocks via the Halevi–Shoup slot-permutation decomposition [25], requiring log2⁡m\log_{2}m rotations per block; see Appendix G.1 for details. For BERT-base with m=128m{=}128 and B=24B{=}24 total blocks across the three edges, this gives 24×7=16824\times 7=168 extra rotations per layer, or 168×2.32168\times 2.32 ms =0.39=0.39 s per layer, totalling 4.7 s over 12 layers. The observed w/o SCP gap is about 12 s, which is larger because the realized remap also includes masking multiplications and recombination additions. The nearly constant slowdown across network profiles confirms that SCP primarily reduces FHE compute rather than communication.

VIII Related Work

We group prior secure machine learning inference systems into three categories: FHE-only, MPC-only, and hybrid FHE–MPC pipelines.

VIII-A FHE-only Secure Inference

CryptoNets pioneered end-to-end leveled-FHE inference by replacing nonlinearities with low-degree polynomials [43]. CHET [44] automates layout selection for CNN inference under FHE. For Transformers, THE-X systematizes polynomial approximations for softmax, layer normalization, and GELU to enable non-interactive BERT inference [13]. CipherFormer [45] extends this to GPT-2 with CKKS packing optimizations. NEXUS [30], THOR [11], and Powerformer [12] further reduce overhead via CKKS-friendly packing, compression, and rotation-efficient attention schedules. A recent survey [46] provides a comprehensive overview of private Transformer inference techniques.

FHE-only inference is non-interactive, but it is constrained by expensive ciphertext key-switching operations such as rotations and relinearization. It also often requires deep multiplicative depth with long modulus chains or heavy bootstrapping.

VIII-B MPC-only Secure Inference

MPC-only systems evaluate the full model on secret shares, using arithmetic protocols for linear layers and specialized sub-protocols for nonlinear operations. SecureML [47], MiniONN [48], ABY [49], and CryptFlow [50] established practical CNN inference with fixed-point arithmetic and mixed-protocol execution. Falcon [51] and XONN [52] explore three-party and binary-circuit alternatives.

For Transformers and LLMs, MPCFormer [53] and follow-on two-party systems co-design efficient protocols for attention, including softmax, GELU, and layer normalization, to scale to large hidden sizes and vocabularies [54, 55, 56, 14, 9, 57, 58]. MPC-only inference requires frequent interaction, so latency and bandwidth can become the bottleneck for deep models and wide activations.

VIII-C Hybrid FHE–MPC Secure Inference

Hybrid systems typically execute wide linear algebra under FHE and delegate nonlinearities and selected reductions to MPC. Gazelle [32] introduced this split for CNNs, while Delphi [59] and Cheetah [31] improved latency through automated partitioning and optimized FHE and MPC building blocks. For Transformers, Iron [15] applies the split to BERT, BOLT [8] improves packing and conversion to avoid bootstrapping while preserving high-accuracy nonlinearities, BumbleBee [16] further optimizes hybrid execution with communication-efficient protocols and GPU-accelerated kernels, and BLB [10] reduces boundary overhead via finer-grained operator fusion and fewer FHE–MPC conversions. Hybrid pipelines balance ciphertext computation with interactive protocols, but they can inherit the overhead of both and are often dominated by additional FHE–MPC conversion costs at the boundaries.

IX Conclusion

We presented EncFormer, a two-party hybrid FHE–MPC framework for private Transformer inference that frames packing, conversion, and nonlinear execution as a single co-design problem. EncFormer uses Stage Compatible Patterns to keep adjacent FHE kernels layout-compatible, a secure complex CKKS–MPC conversion to reduce boundary payload, and a calibrated PhantomFHE decision rule to choose beneficial expanded boundaries.

This design reduces online communication and end-to-end latency across GPT2-base, BERT-base, and BERT-large relative to prior hybrid systems, with average gains of 30.4×\times/9.8×\times against BOLT, 2.6×\times/2.1×\times against BumbleBee, and 1.4×\times/1.3×\times against BLB (communication/latency), while also outperforming FHE-only pipelines on BERT-base under a matched backend. On BERT-base, encrypted inference maintains near-plaintext accuracy on selected GLUE tasks. The broader lesson is that hybrid private inference should be designed around stage compatibility and boundary economics, not primitive choice alone.

IX-A Limitations and Future Work

Like prior systems that rely on surrogate nonlinearities [11, 12, 10], EncFormer still requires task-specific distillation. Extending the framework to settings with less task-specific retraining, stronger malicious-security guarantees, or richer backend-aware boundary models remains important future work.
