Appendix A Additional Details on FHE Kernels

A-A Realization of Ciphertext Shifts

We use the ciphertext shift idea of Jiang et al. [34] and instantiate it under our segment-stacked packing. Under this packing, logical shifts translate into CKKS rotations together with masks, so their cost depends on both rotation distance and the number of masked terms. Algorithms 5 and 6 provide the FHE realizations of the inter-segment shift ΦΔ\Phi^{\Delta} and the intra-segment shift Ψt\Psi^{t}, respectively.

Several kernels also require cyclic wrap-around within only the first LL slots, while keeping slots L,…,n−1L,\dots,n-1 unchanged at zero. For a shift amount τ∈{0,…,L−1}\tau\in\{0,\dots,L-1\}, we use two binary masks 𝐚L,τ\mathbf{a}_{L,\tau} and 𝐛L,τ\mathbf{b}_{L,\tau} to split the first LL slots into the portion that remains in place and the portion that wraps around. Concretely, we set

(𝐚L,τ)i\displaystyle(\mathbf{a}_{L,\tau})_{i} =𝟏{0≤i<L−τ},\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\{0\leq i<L-\tau\},
(𝐛L,τ)i\displaystyle(\mathbf{b}_{L,\tau})_{i} =𝟏{L−τ≤i<L}.\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\{L-\tau\leq i<L\}.

Algorithm 7 realizes this restricted rotation using two CKKS rotations followed by masking and addition.

When only the first C=cusedC=c_{\mathrm{used}} segments are active, meaning L=C​mL=Cm slots, we use the same restricted-rotation primitive to implement wrap-around modulo CC segments. Algorithm 8 defines ΦCΔ\Phi_{C}^{\Delta} by applying 𝖱𝗈𝗍𝖥𝗂𝗋𝗌𝗍C​m\mathsf{RotFirst}_{Cm} with shift Δ​m\Delta m.

A-B Plaintext–Ciphertext Projection Kernel

We follow Section 3.2 for packing, dimensions, and the BSGS accumulation and fold.

A-B1 Plaintext Weights

Under complexification, we use U=⌈G/2⌉U=\lceil G/2\rceil inputs ⟨𝐱~(u)⟩=⟨𝐱(2​u)+i​𝐱(2​u+1)⟩\langle\tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{(u)}\rangle=\langle\mathbf{x}^{(2u)}+i\,\mathbf{x}^{(2u+1)}\rangle and we encode complex weights. Let W¯\bar{W} denote the pre-permuted weight matrix used by this projection kernel. Its columns are ordered to match the target packing of the output. The row index addresses input channels and the column index addresses output channels. For output block bb, giant index pgp_{g}, complex-pair index uu, and baby index qq, the value stored in active segment c∈{0,…,C−1}c\in\{0,\dots,C-1\} is

α⁡(c,q)=(c+q)modC,β⁡(c,pg)=(c−pg​N1)modC.\alpha(c,q)=(c+q)\bmod C,\qquad\beta(c,p_{g})=(c-p_{g}N_{1})\bmod C.

Then

w~u,pg,q(b)​(c)\displaystyle\tilde{w}^{(b)}_{u,p_{g},q}(c) =W¯(2​u)​C+α⁡(c,q),b​C+β⁡(c,pg)\displaystyle=\bar{W}_{(2u)C+\alpha(c,q),\;bC+\beta(c,p_{g})}
−i​W¯(2​u+1)​C+α⁡(c,q),b​C+β⁡(c,pg).\displaystyle-i\,\bar{W}_{(2u+1)C+\alpha(c,q),\;bC+\beta(c,p_{g})}.

All segments c≥Cc\geq C store 00.

Weights are stored as plaintext and can be cheaply pre-permuted to match downstream packing, which only changes plaintext constant construction and adds no FHE cost at inference time. Under segment-column packing, segment cc of ⟨𝐲(b)⟩\langle\mathbf{y}^{(b)}\rangle stores the length mm column Y:,bC+cY_{:,\,bC+c}. A column permutation can therefore be realized by permuting plaintext weight columns so the projection emits YY directly in the target order.

Let d2=H​dhd_{2}=Hd_{h} and index the attention columns by head h∈{0,…,H−1}h\in\{0,\dots,H-1\} and within-head channel u∈{0,…,dh−1}u\in\{0,\dots,d_{h}-1\}. Write the canonical head-major column index as k⁡(h,u)=h​dh+uk(h,u)=hd_{h}+u. For the score kernel, folded-diagonal packing assigns one segment per head, so it is convenient for QQ and KK to place the HH heads next to each other for each fixed uu. We use the score-friendly column order

πS​(h,u)=u​H+h.\pi_{\mathrm{S}}(h,u)=uH+h.

We pre-permute the plaintext weights by permuting columns as

(WQπS)r,πS​(h,u)=(WQ)r,k⁡(h,u),\bigl(W_{Q}^{\pi_{\mathrm{S}}}\bigr)_{r,\,\pi_{\mathrm{S}}(h,u)}=(W_{Q})_{r,\,k(h,u)},
(WKπS)r,πS​(h,u)=(WK)r,k⁡(h,u).\bigl(W_{K}^{\pi_{\mathrm{S}}}\bigr)_{r,\,\pi_{\mathrm{S}}(h,u)}=(W_{K})_{r,\,k(h,u)}.

Then the projection emits Q=A​WQπSQ=AW_{Q}^{\pi_{\mathrm{S}}} and K=A​WKπSK=AW_{K}^{\pi_{\mathrm{S}}} in the score-friendly segment order consumed by the score kernel.

For the value kernel, we use the value-friendly head-major order that keeps channels of the same head together. This aligns them with the head-stacked segments used in the folded-diagonal weights. We set πV​(h,u)=k⁡(h,u)\pi_{\mathrm{V}}(h,u)=k(h,u) and use WVπV=WVW_{V}^{\pi_{\mathrm{V}}}=W_{V}, so the projection emits V=A​WVπVV=AW_{V}^{\pi_{\mathrm{V}}} in head-major order. In all weight-encoding expressions above, the symbol WW refers to the chosen pre-permuted matrix, so no ciphertext repacking is needed between kernels.

A-B2 Key-Switching Complexity

Assuming a precomputed bank of ΦCΔ\Phi_{C}^{\Delta} with cost #​rotbank=O⁡(U​C)\#\textsf{rot}_{\mathrm{bank}}=O(UC) where U=⌈G/2⌉U=\lceil G/2\rceil as in Section 3.2, each ΦCΔ\Phi_{C}^{\Delta} is implemented by 𝖱𝗈𝗍𝖥𝗂𝗋𝗌𝗍C​m\mathsf{RotFirst}_{Cm} and costs two rotations. The total key switching counts are

#​rot=O⁡(Bout​N2),#​conj=O⁡(Bout).\#\textsf{rot}=O(B_{\mathrm{out}}N_{2}),\qquad\#\textsf{conj}=O(B_{\mathrm{out}}).

A-B3 Special Fused Q​KQK Projection

When two projections share the same ciphertext input, most notably Q=A​WQQ=AW_{Q} and K=A​WKK=AW_{K}, we fuse them into one plaintext–ciphertext projection under CKKS complex packing. We construct complex plaintext weights W~\tilde{W} by combining the two real weight matrices after applying the score-friendly column permutation. Formally, we form WQπSW_{Q}^{\pi_{\mathrm{S}}} and WKπSW_{K}^{\pi_{\mathrm{S}}} and encode

W~=WQπS+i​WKπS.\tilde{W}=W_{Q}^{\pi_{\mathrm{S}}}+i\,W_{K}^{\pi_{\mathrm{S}}}.

Running one projection gives Y~=A​W~\tilde{Y}=A\tilde{W} whose real part equals QQ and whose imaginary part equals KK in the score-friendly segment order consumed by the score kernel. Fusion is implemented entirely in plaintext preprocessing, and the ciphertext-side procedure is identical to a single projection. Figure 9 shows a toy example of fused projection and weight pre-permutation.

A-B4 How the SCP Rules Are Satisfied

For V=A​WVV=AW_{V}, the projection emits VV in the head-major packing expected by the value kernel. Concretely, for each output block bb, segment c∈{0,…,C−1}c\in\{0,\dots,C-1\} of ⟨𝐲(b)⟩\langle\mathbf{y}^{(b)}\rangle stores V:,bC+cV_{:,\,bC+c}, so the value kernel consumes the VV ciphertext list directly without any ciphertext-side repacking, satisfying Rule 1. The value kernel consumes the MPC softmax output in minimal folded-diagonal packing, so its MPC-produced input attains Kmin​(P)=⌈H​m22​n⌉K_{\min}(P)=\left\lceil\frac{Hm^{2}}{2n}\right\rceil, satisfying Rule 2.

The value kernel outputs the head-major ciphertext list ⟨Ohm⟩\langle O_{\mathrm{hm}}\rangle. The output projection absorbs the head-major-to-segment-column conversion by pre-permuting its plaintext weight columns (no ciphertext repacking), and therefore consumes ⟨Ohm⟩\langle O_{\mathrm{hm}}\rangle directly, satisfying Rule 1. The output projection is followed by an MPC block, so it exports its output in a minimal packing at the FHE–MPC boundary, satisfying Rule 3.

For the feed-forward network, let X~∈ℝm×d2\tilde{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{2}} denote the activation imported from MPC after LN1, and let H∈ℝm×dffH\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{\mathrm{ff}}} denote the activation output by MPC GELU. Both FF1 and FF2 consume MPC-produced activations and we import them into CKKS in minimal packing, satisfying Rule 2, so the inputs attain Kmin​(X~)=⌈m​d22​n⌉K_{\min}(\tilde{X})=\left\lceil\frac{md_{2}}{2n}\right\rceil and Kmin​(H)=⌈m​dff2​n⌉K_{\min}(H)=\left\lceil\frac{md_{\mathrm{ff}}}{2n}\right\rceil. FF1 computes the pre-activation G=X~​W1∈ℝm×dffG=\tilde{X}W_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{\mathrm{ff}}} and is followed by MPC GELU, so it exports GG in minimal packing, satisfying Rule 3, with Kmin​(G)=⌈m​dff2​n⌉K_{\min}(G)=\left\lceil\frac{md_{\mathrm{ff}}}{2n}\right\rceil. FF2 computes X~′=H​W2∈ℝm×d2\tilde{X}^{\prime}=HW_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{2}} and is followed by an MPC block, so it exports X~′\tilde{X}^{\prime} in minimal packing, satisfying Rule 3, with Kmin​(X~′)=⌈m​d22​n⌉K_{\min}(\tilde{X}^{\prime})=\left\lceil\frac{md_{2}}{2n}\right\rceil.

A-C Ciphertext–Ciphertext Attention Kernels

We follow Section 3.3 for the kernel structure and notation.

A-C1 Score Kernel Packing

For each t∈{0,…,m/2−1}t\in\{0,\dots,m/2-1\}, the score kernel outputs a folded-diagonal ciphertext ⟨𝐒t⟩\langle\mathbf{S}_{t}\rangle. Only the first H​mHm slots are informative after head reduction, phase alignment, and undoing the baby shift. Let cut⁡(⟨𝐱⟩)\mathrm{cut}(\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle) denote the first H​mHm slots of ⟨𝐱⟩\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle and define the exported stream 𝐬=cut⁡(⟨𝐒0⟩)​‖⋯‖​cut​(⟨𝐒m/2−1⟩)\mathbf{s}=\mathrm{cut}(\langle\mathbf{S}_{0}\rangle)\|\cdots\|\mathrm{cut}(\langle\mathbf{S}_{m/2-1}\rangle). We pack 𝐬\mathbf{s} sequentially into the minimal number of ciphertexts Kmin​(S)=⌈H​m22​n⌉K_{\min}(S)=\left\lceil\frac{Hm^{2}}{2n}\right\rceil (here N⁡(S)=H​m2N(S)=Hm^{2} because the score matrix has HH heads each containing m2m^{2} entries, and complex packing stores two real values per slot), satisfying Rule 3 of SCP.

A-C2 Value Kernel Packing

MPC returns the post-softmax weights in the same minimal folded-diagonal export order as above, namely as the stream 𝐩=cut⁡(⟨𝐏0⟩)​‖⋯‖​cut​(⟨𝐏m/2−1⟩)\mathbf{p}=\mathrm{cut}(\langle\mathbf{P}_{0}\rangle)\|\cdots\|\mathrm{cut}(\langle\mathbf{P}_{m/2-1}\rangle) packed into Kmin​(P)=⌈H​m22​n⌉K_{\min}(P)=\left\lceil\frac{Hm^{2}}{2n}\right\rceil ciphertexts. Let HblkH_{\mathrm{blk}} be the number of heads packed per value ciphertext and let BV=⌈H/Hblk⌉B_{V}=\lceil H/H_{\mathrm{blk}}\rceil. Under the standard setting dh=m/2=64d_{h}=m/2=64 used in our implementation, this minimal stream reshapes directly into a head-major folded-diagonal ciphertext list

⟨Pfd⟩={⟨𝐩fd(ℓ)⟩}ℓ=0BV−1.\langle P_{\mathrm{fd}}\rangle=\{\langle\mathbf{p}^{(\ell)}_{\mathrm{fd}}\rangle\}_{\ell=0}^{B_{V}-1}.

Within block ℓ\ell, segment

k⁡(h~,t)=h~​(m/2)+tk(\tilde{h},t)=\tilde{h}\,(m/2)+t

with h~∈{0,…,Hblk−1}\tilde{h}\in\{0,\dots,H_{\mathrm{blk}}-1\} and t∈{0,…,m/2−1}t\in\{0,\dots,m/2-1\} stores the diagonal pair

pt(ℓ,h~)+i​pt+m/2(ℓ,h~).p_{t}^{(\ell,\tilde{h})}+i\,p_{t+m/2}^{(\ell,\tilde{h})}.

This is exactly the representation consumed by the value kernel, so the MPC–FHE boundary remains minimal and satisfies Rule 2 of SCP.

A-C3 Score Kernel Block Phase Correction

Block ℓ\ell has head phase rℓ=(ℓ​C)modHr_{\ell}=(\ell C)\bmod H. When C≢0(modH)C\not\equiv 0\pmod{H}, different blocks start at different head offsets. We sum score contributions by phase and align them inside the first H​mHm slots. For r∈{0,…,H−1}r\in\{0,\dots,H-1\} define

𝖠𝗅𝗂𝗀𝗇r​(⟨𝐱⟩)=𝖱𝗈𝗍𝖥𝗂𝗋𝗌𝗍H​m​(⟨𝐱⟩,(H−r)​m).\mathsf{Align}_{r}\!\left(\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle\right)=\mathsf{RotFirst}_{Hm}\!\left(\langle\mathbf{x}\rangle,(H-r)m\right).

We apply 𝖠𝗅𝗂𝗀𝗇r\mathsf{Align}_{r} before combining phases to form ⟨𝐒t⟩\langle\mathbf{S}_{t}\rangle.

A-C4 Mask Construction

Let 𝐞s\mathbf{e}_{s} be the binary plaintext mask that is one on the mm slots of segment ss and zero elsewhere. For the score kernel routing step, we use disjoint active-segment masks {𝐦c}c=0C−1\{\mathbf{m}_{c}\}_{c=0}^{C-1}. When the first CC segments are active, we set 𝐦c=𝐞c\mathbf{m}_{c}=\mathbf{e}_{c}.

In the head-major layout, each ciphertext block packs HblkH_{\mathrm{blk}} heads contiguously. Segment k⁡(h~,u)=h~​dh+uk(\tilde{h},u)=\tilde{h}\,d_{h}+u stores channel u∈{0,…,dh−1}u\in\{0,\dots,d_{h}-1\} of local head h~∈{0,…,Hblk−1}\tilde{h}\in\{0,\dots,H_{\mathrm{blk}}-1\}. For the value-kernel broadcast step, define the channel mask

𝐧u=∑h~=0Hblk−1𝐞h~​dh+u,u=0,…,dh−1.\mathbf{n}_{u}=\sum_{\tilde{h}=0}^{H_{\mathrm{blk}}-1}\mathbf{e}_{\tilde{h}\,d_{h}+u},\qquad u=0,\dots,d_{h}-1.

This mask keeps exactly the segments with within-head channel offset uu across all local heads in the block. The value kernel output remains in head-major layout; the subsequent output projection absorbs the layout conversion via weight pre-permutation (no explicit FHE remap stage).

A-C5 Key Switching Complexity

Let B=⌈d/C⌉B=\lceil d/C\rceil and BV=⌈H/Hblk⌉B_{V}=\lceil H/H_{\mathrm{blk}}\rceil, where CC is the channel capacity per ciphertext and HblkH_{\mathrm{blk}} is the number of heads packed per ciphertext block. Both kernels use precomputed Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi banks.

For the score kernel, each of the m/2m/2 diagonals multiplies BB channel blocks. Rotations are dominated by Ψ\Psi-bank construction and the per-diagonal postprocessing.

#​ctmulS=#​relinS\displaystyle\#\textsf{ctmul}_{S}=\#\textsf{relin}_{S} =O⁡(m​B),\displaystyle=O(mB),
#​rotS\displaystyle\#\textsf{rot}_{S} =O⁡(B⁡(β+g)+m​log⁡C).\displaystyle=O\bigl(B(\beta+g)+m\log C\bigr).

For BERT-base with B=7B=7, β=16\beta=16, g=8g=8, m=128m=128, C=120C=120, and caching of repeated shifts, the implementation measures 630 rotations and 448 ct-ct multiplications (Table 2).

For the value kernel, each of the m/2m/2 offsets uses BVB_{V} head blocks. Rotations are dominated by the token-shift Ψ\Psi bank over mm offsets and the Φ\Phi broadcasts over O⁡(dh)O(d_{h}) segment shifts per block.

#​ctmulV=#​relinV\displaystyle\#\textsf{ctmul}_{V}=\#\textsf{relin}_{V} =O⁡(m​BV),\displaystyle=O(mB_{V}),
#​rotV\displaystyle\#\textsf{rot}_{V} =O⁡(BV​(m+dh)).\displaystyle=O\bigl(B_{V}(m+d_{h})\bigr).

For BERT-base with BV=6B_{V}=6, m=128m=128, dh=64d_{h}=64, the implementation measures 1524 rotations and 384 ct-ct multiplications.

A-C6 Why the KS Counts Differ from Powerformer

Powerformer [12] accelerates attention by applying complex packing to a generic blockwise CCMM under modified column packing. Its blockwise transforms σ~,τ~,ϕ~,ψ~\tilde{\sigma},\tilde{\tau},\tilde{\phi},\tilde{\psi} and auxiliary routines such as BlockTrans, BlockTau, BlockSigma, Extract, and SplitPaste remain part of the algorithmic skeleton; complex arithmetic mainly reduces the number of calls to these routines by evaluating paired operands together. In that sense, the gain is a constant-factor reduction within the generic CCMM framework rather than a change to the object being computed.

By contrast, EncFormer rewrites attention around the structure of the desired outputs. For the score matrix, we do not first form a generic packed product and then extract the needed diagonals. Instead, for t=j​β+st=j\beta+s we directly produce the folded pair (t,t+m/2)(t,t+m/2) by

⟨𝐮t⟩=∑ℓ⟨𝐪−s(ℓ)⟩⊙(⟨𝐤j​β(ℓ)⟩+i⁡⟨𝐤m/2+j​β(ℓ)⟩).\langle\mathbf{u}_{t}\rangle=\sum_{\ell}\langle\mathbf{q}^{(\ell)}_{-s}\rangle\odot\bigl(\langle\mathbf{k}^{(\ell)}_{j\beta}\rangle+i\,\langle\mathbf{k}^{(\ell)}_{m/2+j\beta}\rangle\bigr).

One complex ctmul therefore produces two diagonals at once, and the required shifts come from reusable Ψ\Psi-banks of sizes β\beta and g=m/βg=m/\beta rather than from a full blockwise permutation-and-extraction pipeline. This is why the score kernel scales as #​ctmulS=O⁡(m​B)\#\textsf{ctmul}_{S}=O(mB) and #​rotS=O⁡(B⁡(β+g)+m​log⁡C)\#\textsf{rot}_{S}=O(B(\beta+g)+m\log C).

For the value kernel, we again avoid a generic CCMM by using the token-shift identity

⟨𝐮(ℓ)⟩=⟨𝐯(ℓ)⟩−i​Ψm/2​(⟨𝐯(ℓ)⟩),\langle\mathbf{u}^{(\ell)}\rangle=\langle\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}\rangle-i\,\Psi^{m/2}\!\bigl(\langle\mathbf{v}^{(\ell)}\rangle\bigr),

so that the offset pair (t,t+m/2)(t,t+m/2) is handled by one complex operand ⟨𝐮t(ℓ)⟩=Ψ−t​(⟨𝐮(ℓ)⟩)\langle\mathbf{u}^{(\ell)}_{t}\rangle=\Psi^{-t}(\langle\mathbf{u}^{(\ell)}\rangle). This halves the token-shift bank from mm offsets to m/2m/2 effective complex pairs, and the folded-diagonal weights are broadcast with simple head-major masks instead of generic block transforms. The resulting complexity is #​ctmulV=O⁡(m​BV)\#\textsf{ctmul}_{V}=O(mB_{V}) and #​rotV=O⁡(BV​(m+dh))\#\textsf{rot}_{V}=O(B_{V}(m+d_{h})).

The key point is therefore structural: Powerformer obtains a constant-factor compression of a generic matrix-multiplication pipeline, whereas EncFormer rewrites attention into diagonal-pair and token-shift-pair primitives that match the geometry of Q​K⊤QK^{\top} and P​VPV. Together with SCP eliminating post-kernel remaps, this is the main reason Table 2 shows substantially lower weighted primitive cost for EncFormer than for Powerformer.

Appendix B Protocols for GELU

We employ the GELU approximation and secure evaluation protocol from BOLT [8]. The approximation is a three-branch piecewise function that saturates outside a bounded region and uses a low-degree polynomial inside. Intuitively, values far in the positive tail are passed through unchanged, values far in the negative tail are clamped to zero, and only the mid-range requires a nontrivial computation. This structure is well-suited to MPC because it reduces the expensive arithmetic to the interval where GELU is most nonlinear, while the outer branches are implemented by inexpensive conditional selection.

For x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R},

ApproxGELU⁡(x)={x,x>2.7,a​|x|4+b​|x|3+c​|x|2+d​|x|+e+0.5​x,|x|≤2.7,0,x<−2.7.\mathrm{ApproxGELU}(x)=\begin{cases}x,&x>2.7,\\ \begin{aligned} a|x|^{4}+b|x|^{3}+c|x|^{2}\\ {}+d|x|+e+0.5x,\end{aligned}&|x|\leq 2.7,\\ 0,&x<-2.7.\end{cases} (7)

We follow the same MPC notation and primitives as in Section 4.1. In particular, values are represented as additive shares over ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}} and XOR-shared bits, and the protocol uses the standard comparison and multiplexing primitives to implement slotwise branching. Let 𝐱(0),𝐱(1)∈ℝn\mathbf{x}^{(0)},\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and pack 𝐱ℂ=𝐱(0)+i​𝐱(1)\mathbf{x}^{\mathbb{C}}=\mathbf{x}^{(0)}+i\mathbf{x}^{(1)}.

Our complex conversion in Section 5 exports the real and imaginary channels in one invocation of ΠC2Mℂ\Pi_{\mathrm{C2M}}^{\mathbb{C}} and packs the two MPC outputs back with ΠM2Cℂ\Pi_{\mathrm{M2C}}^{\mathbb{C}}.

Within MPC, the key idea is to evaluate the polynomial branch using ordinary arithmetic on shared values, while using comparisons and multiplexing to select the correct branch for each slot. The absolute value in the mid-range polynomial is handled by first determining the sign of each slot and then choosing between two sign-specialized polynomials that are identical up to the sign of the odd-degree terms. This avoids an explicit absolute-value circuit and reduces the branching logic to a small number of comparisons and multiplexers.

For j∈{0,1}j\in\{0,1\}, define candidate vectors

𝐅0(j)\displaystyle\mathbf{F}_{0}^{(j)} =a​(𝐱(j))4−b​(𝐱(j))3+c​(𝐱(j))2+(0.5−d)​𝐱(j)+e,\displaystyle=a(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{4}-b(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{3}+c(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{2}+(0.5-d)\mathbf{x}^{(j)}+e, (8)
𝐅1(j)\displaystyle\mathbf{F}_{1}^{(j)} =a​(𝐱(j))4+b​(𝐱(j))3+c​(𝐱(j))2+(0.5+d)​𝐱(j)+e.\displaystyle=a(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{4}+b(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{3}+c(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})^{2}+(0.5+d)\mathbf{x}^{(j)}+e.

We use the same polynomial coefficients (a,b,c,d,e)(a,b,c,d,e) as reported in BOLT [8].

In an alternative pipeline, we evaluate the mid-range polynomial branch entirely in MPC after a single complex CKKS-to-MPC conversion and then convert the final outputs back to CKKS, as shown in Algorithm 10.

Appendix C Ring and Field Conversion

We describe two-party primitives for converting additive shares between an odd-modulus ring ℤq\mathbb{Z}_{q} and a power-of-two ring ℤ2ℓ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell}}, following the extension-based approach of BOLT, SiRNN, and BLB [8, 60, 10]. In EncFormer, qq is the CKKS ciphertext modulus at the conversion boundary, i.e., q=QLconvq=Q_{L_{\mathrm{conv}}}. For additive sharing over ℤM\mathbb{Z}_{M}, we write [[u]]M[[u]]_{M} where u0+u1≡u(modM)u_{0}+u_{1}\equiv u\pmod{M}. We interpret ring elements with signed fixed-point semantics via the centered representative clM(u)∈(−M/2,M/2]\mathrm{cl}_{M}(u)\in(-M/2,M/2], defined as the unique integer congruent to umodMu\bmod M that lies in this interval. We use a signed extension protocol ΠExt\Pi_{\mathrm{Ext}} that lifts shares to a larger power-of-two ring while preserving clM​(⋅)\mathrm{cl}_{M}(\cdot) except with probability at most 2−σ2^{-\sigma}.

C-A Field-to-ring conversion

ΠField2Ring\Pi_{\mathrm{Field2Ring}} converts [[x]]q[[x]]_{q} to [[x]]2ℓ[[x]]_{2^{\ell}}. Invoke ΠExtq,2ℓ′\Pi^{q,2^{\ell^{\prime}}}_{\mathrm{Ext}} with ℓ′≥max⁡(⌈log2⁡q⌉,ℓ)\ell^{\prime}\geq\max(\lceil\log_{2}q\rceil,\ell) to obtain shares in ℤ2ℓ′\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell^{\prime}}} that represent clq​(x)\mathrm{cl}_{q}(x) (with error ≤2−σ\leq 2^{-\sigma}), then each party locally reduces its share modulo 2ℓ2^{\ell}. We choose ℓ\ell so that all valid values satisfy |clq​(x)|<2ℓ−1|\mathrm{cl}_{q}(x)|<2^{\ell-1}.

C-B Ring-to-field conversion

ΠRing2Field\Pi_{\mathrm{Ring2Field}} converts [[m]]2ℓ[[m]]_{2^{\ell}} to [[m]]q[[m]]_{q}. Invoke ΠExt\Pi_{\mathrm{Ext}} to lift to ℤ2ℓ+σ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell+\sigma}}, obtaining representatives m0′,m1′∈[0,2ℓ+σ)m^{\prime}_{0},m^{\prime}_{1}\in[0,2^{\ell+\sigma}) such that, except with probability 2−σ2^{-\sigma}, the integer sum satisfies

m0′+m1′=2ℓ+σ+cl2ℓ​(m).m^{\prime}_{0}+m^{\prime}_{1}=2^{\ell+\sigma}+\mathrm{cl}_{2^{\ell}}(m).

(The 2ℓ+σ2^{\ell+\sigma} offset encodes the signed value as a non-negative representative in ℤ2ℓ+σ\mathbb{Z}_{2^{\ell+\sigma}}.) Each party then maps locally into ℤq\mathbb{Z}_{q} by

[[m]]0(q)=m0′modq,[[m]]1(q)=(m1′−2ℓ+σ)modq,[[m]]^{(q)}_{0}=m^{\prime}_{0}\bmod q,\qquad[[m]]^{(q)}_{1}=(m^{\prime}_{1}-2^{\ell+\sigma})\bmod q,

so that [[m]]0(q)+[[m]]1(q)≡cl2ℓ​(m)(modq)[[m]]^{(q)}_{0}+[[m]]^{(q)}_{1}\equiv\mathrm{cl}_{2^{\ell}}(m)\pmod{q} except with probability 2−σ2^{-\sigma}.

C-C Security

Both conversions consist of one invocation of ΠExt\Pi_{\mathrm{Ext}} followed by local computations. If ΠExt\Pi_{\mathrm{Ext}} is simulation-secure, then the conversion view can be simulated from the input/output shares, leaking nothing beyond public parameters, up to statistical error 2−σ2^{-\sigma}.

Appendix D Cost Analysis Model Discussion

We use the latency decomposition in Eq. (3) and the decision rule in Eq. (4) to compare boundary choices via Δ​Tconv\Delta T_{\text{conv}} and Δ​Tcomp\Delta T_{\text{comp}}. A boundary change can trade off two effects: it can reduce computation time by moving operators to the cheaper domain, and it can increase or decrease the conversion overhead at domain boundaries. These effects are captured by Δ​Tcomp\Delta T_{\text{comp}} and Δ​Tconv\Delta T_{\text{conv}}, respectively.

The minimal-conversion baseline BB defined in Section 5.1 serves as a normalization reference for boundary payload under a fixed tensor shape. It does not claim to minimize end-to-end latency and is not an optimizer by itself. We use Eq. (4) as a screening tool to estimate the sign of the latency change when moving from BB to a candidate design DD.

To illustrate how the cost model can guide boundary placement, we apply it to the GELU boundary decision under PhantomFHE across 12 instances: 3 models ×\times 4 network profiles. The model estimates “Expand” for all BERT-large profiles and for WAN2/WAN3 on BERT-base and GPT2-base, and “Minimal” for LAN/WAN1 on the smaller models — a non-trivial 8/4 split that illustrates the model can surface trade-offs varying across deployment settings. We note that Δ​Tckks\Delta T_{\text{ckks}} and CroundC_{\text{round}} are measured under specific backend and network conditions, so the model’s estimates should be treated as directional rather than precise.

In practice, TmpcT_{\text{mpc}} can also vary across network profiles because interactive MPC primitives are communication-bound. As bandwidth decreases or round-trip latency increases, the pipeline can shift from compute-dominated to message-dominated behavior, which changes the relative weight of Δ​Tconv\Delta T_{\text{conv}} and Δ​Tcomp\Delta T_{\text{comp}}. Since the deployment network may be unknown at design time, we recommend evaluating candidate boundary placements across multiple network profiles before committing to a design.

Appendix E MPC Round Count Comparison

Table XII compares interactive MPC rounds per layer. FHE-only systems (THOR, Powerformer) use zero MPC rounds but require bootstrapping. The BOLT and BLB counts are analytically derived from their published protocol descriptions. BOLT’s softmax uses 6 rounds (tree max-finding for L=64L{=}64). BLB adopts BumbleBee’s softmax protocol [16], which requires 18 rounds: ⌈log2⁡L⌉\lceil\log_{2}L\rceil rounds for tree max-finding (L=128L{=}128), 6 sequential squarings for negExp, plus comparison, mux, reciprocal, and scaling. EncFormer uses MBMax (3 rounds) and BOLT-style GELU (4 rounds); MBLN requires zero interactive rounds because rowsum, broadcast, and affine scaling are all local operations on additive shares.

Appendix F Proof of Proposition 1

Proof.

(i) Zero remap. SCP matches all three direct FHE–FHE edges (QKV→\toScore, QKV→\toValue, Value→\toOUT) via weight pre-permutation, and the three MPC-boundary edges satisfy Rules 2 and 3 with minimal packing. Any alternative assignment that changes a producer–consumer matching on an FHE–FHE edge necessarily introduces out⁡(Ki)≠in⁡(Kj)\mathrm{out}(K_{i})\neq\mathrm{in}(K_{j}), since no other packing in ℱ\mathcal{F} satisfies the consumer kernel without repacking.

Ω⁡(m​log⁡m)\Omega(m\log m) rotation lower bound. A remap between two distinct packings in ℱ\mathcal{F} requires a general slot permutation on each ciphertext block. In the segment-column layout with mm rows, the permutation acts on mm slot groups. By the Halevi–Shoup decomposition [25], any such permutation requires at least log2⁡m\log_{2}m Galois automorphisms (rotations), each involving a key-switching operation. With BB ciphertext blocks affected per edge, the total cost is B⋅log2⁡mB\cdot\log_{2}m rotations per edge, giving Ω⁡(m​log⁡m)\Omega(m\log m) across the Θ⁡(m)\Theta(m) affected slots per block.

(ii) Minimal boundary count. At each FHE–MPC boundary, Rules 2 and 3 require that ciphertexts use minimal packing with KminK_{\min} ciphertexts. Any expanded packing uses K>KminK>K_{\min} ciphertexts, each of which must pass through the conversion protocol, increasing boundary communication proportionally.

Quantitative example. For BERT-base (m=128m{=}128, C=128C{=}128, log2⁡m=7\log_{2}m{=}7), disabling SCP adds 168 extra rotations per layer across the three FHE–FHE edges (2424 blocks ×\times 77 rotations), or ∼0.39{\sim}0.39 s per layer (∼9%{\sim}9\% of per-layer FHE time). ∎

Appendix G SCP Edge Analysis for All Models

Table XIII extends the BERT-base SCP analysis from the main text to all three evaluated models. Without SCP, each direct FHE–FHE edge requires log2⁡m\log_{2}m rotations per ciphertext block for slot permutation. MPC-boundary edges incur no FHE remapping because MPC resets the data format.

The observed overhead is 2.6–7.7×\times the rotation-only prediction because the actual slot permutation also involves plaintext-multiply masking and ciphertext addition for recombination, which are O⁡(1)O(1) per rotation but not counted in the rotation proxy.

G-A Repacking Algorithm in the w/o SCP Ablation

Halevi–Shoup slot-permutation decomposition. Applying an arbitrary permutation to the slots of a CKKS ciphertext cannot be done in a single operation. Halevi and Shoup [25] show that any target slot permutation π\pi can be expressed as a linear combination of rotations:

Repack⁡(⟨𝐯⟩)=∑k=0log2⁡m−1Rot⁡(⟨𝐯⟩, 2k)⋅𝐦k,\mathrm{Repack}(\langle\mathbf{v}\rangle)=\sum_{k=0}^{\log_{2}m-1}\mathrm{Rot}\!\left(\langle\mathbf{v}\rangle,\,2^{k}\right)\cdot\mathbf{m}_{k},

where each 𝐦k\mathbf{m}_{k} is a plaintext binary mask that selects the slots whose target position is reached by a rotation of 2k2^{k}. This decomposes the permutation into log2⁡m\log_{2}m rotation–mask–accumulate (RMA) steps. Each RMA step requires one key-switched rotation, one plaintext multiplication, and one ciphertext addition, giving log2⁡m\log_{2}m rotations, log2⁡m\log_{2}m plaintext multiplications, and log2⁡m\log_{2}m additions per ciphertext block.

In the w/o SCP ablation (Table 11), we insert a generic slot-permutation repack at every direct FHE–FHE edge. The repacking converts one packing format to another by cycling through log2⁡m\log_{2}m RMA steps as described above.

Concretely, the ablation inserts repacking at the three direct FHE–FHE edges per layer identified in Section 3.1.1: (1) QKV→\toScore remaps Q and K from segment-column to the score-friendly layout (2×⌈d/C⌉2\times\lceil d/C\rceil blocks, log2⁡m\log_{2}m rotations each); (2) QKV→\toValue remaps V from segment-column to head-major order (⌈d/C⌉\lceil d/C\rceil blocks); and (3) Value→\toOUT remaps the value output from head-major to segment-column (⌈d/C⌉\lceil d/C\rceil blocks). Edges that cross an MPC boundary (e.g. Score→\toSoftmax, OUT→\toLN) are not affected because MPC resets the data format via decryption and re-encryption. The total rotation count per layer is the sum reported in Table XIII. The observed latency gap exceeds the rotation-only estimate because each rotation step is accompanied by a masking multiplication and an accumulation addition, and the large number of sequential CKKS operations incurs additional GPU kernel-launch and memory-transfer overhead.

Appendix H Cost Model Validation Details

H-A GELU Boundary Predictions

Table XIV summarizes the cost model’s boundary decision across both backends. PhantomFHE produces a non-trivial 8/4 split, while Liberate.FHE predicts Minimal for all 12 cases due to its 18×18\times higher CKKS compute time. Table XV provides the full per-instance breakdown for PhantomFHE.

Table XV reports the full prediction-vs-observation validation for the GELU boundary decision under PhantomFHE. The model estimates “Expand” for 8 instances and “Minimal” for 4, namely LAN/WAN1 on BERT-base and GPT2-base, and the estimates agree with the observed latency direction in all cases. The tightest positive margin is on WAN2 GPT2-base (Δ​T=−42\Delta T=-42 ms), while the tightest negative margin is on WAN1 GPT2-base (Δ​T=+52\Delta T=+52 ms).

H-B Liberate.FHE Decision Boundary

The cost model includes the CKKS pre-evaluation cost of the GELU polynomial candidates F0F_{0} and F1F_{1} as a negative Δctmul\Delta_{\mathrm{ctmul}} term in Eq. Eq. (6). Each degree-5 polynomial evaluation requires 3 ctmuls per complex ciphertext block, giving 6​⌈Bff/2⌉6\lceil B_{\mathrm{ff}}/2\rceil extra ctmuls total (e.g., 72 for BERT-base). Under PhantomFHE (tctmul=2.65t_{\mathrm{ctmul}}=2.65 ms), this adds only ∼\sim0.19 s and is outweighed by MPC round savings on higher-latency profiles. Under Liberate.FHE (tctmul=48.66t_{\mathrm{ctmul}}=48.66 ms, 18×18\times PhantomFHE), the same 72 ctmuls cost ∼\sim3.5 s, far exceeding MPC savings, so all 12 Liberate instances correctly predict “Minimal.” This backend-dependent discrimination validates that the model captures a real trade-off rather than a degenerate one.

Appendix I Total Communication Including Conversion Payload

Cross-paper comparison note. We follow the cross-paper comparison methodology commonly used in this area: the baseline metrics reported throughout this paper are taken from the corresponding publications under their stated experimental settings, and our claims against prior hybrid systems should be interpreted in that sense rather than as a controlled re-implementation on a single platform. Because each prior system uses its own CKKS library, GPU hardware, and MPC implementation, a fully matched head-to-head rerun is often infeasible. Likewise, our WAN latency figures are obtained by applying an analytical network overlay to measured communication volume and MPC round counts, rather than by cross-site deployment; this is the same evaluation methodology adopted by prior hybrid Transformer systems such as BOLT, BumbleBee, and BLB. Section 7.3 therefore complements the main comparison with a matched-backend study that isolates library effects.

Table XVI estimates total communication (online MPC traffic plus FHE–MPC conversion payload) for BERT-base. The conversion payload per layer is computed from the ciphertext counts in Table 4 at 256 KB per ciphertext (n=16384n=16384, ∼\sim15 RNS primes). For all systems, conversion payload is small relative to online MPC traffic (0.2–0.5 GB vs. 2–64 GB), so the relative ranking is preserved under total communication.

Appendix J Additional Generality Examples

The SCP packing rules and the boundary cost model are stated in terms of kernel composition rather than Transformer-specific semantics. To illustrate this, we apply the same reasoning to two analytical examples.

J-A 2-Layer CNN

Consider a CNN with Conv1 (3×33\times 3, 16 filters) →\to ReLU →\to Conv2 (3×33\times 3, 32 filters) →\to ReLU →\to FC, operating on 28×2828\times 28 input images with n=8192n=8192 CKKS slots. Conv1 uses 144 rotations (9×169\times 16), Conv2 uses 288 rotations (9×329\times 32), and the FC layer uses 10 rotations. Without co-designed packing, the Conv1→\toReLU and Conv2→\toReLU boundaries each require repacking (6 ciphertext blocks total), costing ∼\sim14 ms under PhantomFHE primitive latencies.

J-B 3-Layer MLP

Consider an MLP with FC1 (768→3072768\to 3072) →\to GELU →\to FC2 (3072→30723072\to 3072) →\to GELU →\to FC3 (3072→7683072\to 768), using n=16384n=16384 slots and m=128m=128, matching the BERT-base hidden and FFN dimensions. With C=128C=128 segments per ciphertext, FC1 and FC2 each produce ⌈3072/128⌉=24\lceil 3072/128\rceil=24 output blocks. Without co-designed packing, FC1→\toGELU and FC2→\toGELU require repacking 48 blocks at log2⁡(128)=7\log_{2}(128)=7 rotations each, totaling 336 extra rotations (∼\sim111 ms). With the GELU boundary cost model, each GELU block also admits an “Expand” option analogous to the Transformer GELU pre-evaluation, saving 3 MPC rounds per block at the cost of 2×8=162\times 8=16 extra complex ciphertexts per GELU.

These examples are analytical illustrations; full empirical evaluation on non-Transformer workloads is left to future work.

Appendix K Powerformer-Style Distillation

For each GLUE task, we fine-tune a plaintext BERT-base teacher with standard nonlinearities following Powerformer [12]. We then distill an HE-compatible student that keeps the same macro-architecture but replaces all nonlinear components with the approximations used in our protocol. Distillation helps the student adapt to the changed activation and normalization behavior introduced by these approximations while preserving task accuracy.

Let the teacher be ft​(x,Wt)f_{t}(x;W_{t}) and the student be fs​(x,Ws,θ)f_{s}(x;W_{s},\theta). For input xx with label yy and logits zt,zsz_{t},z_{s}, we minimize

ℒ\displaystyle\mathcal{L} =λsup​ℒCE​(zs,y)+λkd​ℒKD​(zs,zt)\displaystyle=\lambda_{\mathrm{sup}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(z_{s},y)+\lambda_{\mathrm{kd}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}(z_{s},z_{t})
+λint∑ℓ∈𝒮‖hs(ℓ)−ht(ℓ)‖22.\displaystyle\quad+\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{S}}\left\lVert h^{(\ell)}_{s}-h^{(\ell)}_{t}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

where hs(ℓ),ht(ℓ)h^{(\ell)}_{s},h^{(\ell)}_{t} are matched intermediate tensors and 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the set of layers used. The logit distillation term uses temperature TT

ℒKD(zs,zt)=T2KL(softmax(ztT)∥softmax(zsT)).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}(z_{s},z_{t})=T^{2}\ \mathrm{KL}\!\left(\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{z_{t}}{T}\right)\ \bigg\|\ \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{z_{s}}{T}\right)\right).

In EncFormer, we learn the Softmax and LayerNorm parameters θ\theta jointly with student weights WsW_{s} during distillation, and deploy (Ws,θ)(W_{s},\theta) unchanged for encrypted inference. We follow Powerformer-style hyperparameters with batch size 64 and learning rate 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}. We also use early stopping with an extended distillation budget and seeds {0,42,777}\{0,42,777\}.
